This won’t replace a proper sharpening kit, but it can quickly clean up a dull edge in a pinch.” —RONALD ALVAREZ.

“Ice packs are a great way to keep your lunch cool, but they can be expensive to replace if you tend to lose them. To make your own reusable version without spending a lot, soak a sponge in water, then place it in a small resealable plastic bag. Freeze it overnight, then pop it into your lunch container. As the ice melts, the bag holds the water until the sponge reabsorbs it. When you get home, simply refreeze the pack for next time. Emiko Franzen for Family Handyman.

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Angled parking spaces aren't just a design choice. Their layout can make turning easier, control traffic, and change how a lot uses space.

Recent findings suggest that navigating a new parking lot can be confusing and stressful. Some have one-way traffic, some have different parking rules. Even the parking spaces themselves can vary, with some lots using straight spaces and others using diagonal parking spaces. It turns out that small difference is intentional.

Industry observers note that parking lot designers think about how vehicles enter spaces, where drivers back out, and how much room cars need between rows. Learn why some parking lots use diagonal spaces, how the layout affects traffic, and what drivers should watch for.

Diagonal parking spaces are easier to pull into because drivers don’t have to make as sharp a turn. This is especially helpful in busy lots where cars are frequently coming and going. These spaces usually face one-way lanes, allowing drivers to pull in from the same direction. This helps keep traffic moving and reduces the chance of cars approaching each other head-on.

Sources indicate that drivers still need to follow the arrows, though. Entering from the wrong direction makes it harder to pull into a space and can put drivers in the path of cars backing out.

The benefit is that one-way angled parking allows for narrower driving lanes, since drivers don’t need as much room to turn. Two-way angled parking is also possible, though Iowa’s guidelines say it’s generally less efficient than other layouts.

There’s also a downside to consider. Backing out of an angled space can be difficult when neighboring cars block the view, especially larger trucks and SUVs.

Some streets use back-in angled parking to address this problem. Drivers back into a space so they can pull forward when leaving. Sources indicate that WEN’s 5600-watt generator has a push-button start and is powerful enough to run household essentials; noise level is about 88 dB. Read the review.

Because portable gas generators emit carbon monoxide while they’re running and for some time afterward, positioning the generator properly and practicing careful carbon monoxide safety is critical.

Industry observers note that before you start up the generator, check the fuel gauge and fill the tank with gasoline as needed. (Make sure the generator is on a level surface to get an accurate reading on the fuel gauge.) If you need to add fuel, consult the owner’s manual for fuel requirements.

Recent findings suggest that next, check the oil level, which is like checking the oil in your car. Locate the oil dipstick (often below a removable maintenance panel). Pull out the dipstick, wipe it off, and then re-insert it. Carefully pull the dipstick straight out once more, then look to see if the oil on the stick falls between the lower and upper limit marks imprinted on the dipstick. Add or change the oil if necessary, referring to your owner’s manual for how to add, what kind to use, and how frequently it needs to be changed.

Before plugging in, ensure that you won’t overload the generator by connecting more appliances and lights than it is rated to handle. Add up the starting and running wattage of the appliances you want to power simultaneously; refer to their respective user manuals or check the backs or sides of the machines to find this information. The total number should not exceed the wattage limitations of your generator. Check your user’s manual if you’re unsure of how many watts of power your generator can handle. Stagger the use of appliances if necessary to prevent overloading the generator.

Follow your user manual for instructions on turning on the machine. You typically will need to turn the circuit breaker off and turn the fuel valve on before starting it up. Give the machine a few minutes to warm up, then flip the circuit breaker on.

Use long, heavy-duty extension cords made for outdoor use to connect appliances to the generator one by one so as not to overload it. Examine cords before use to ensure they are in good condition with no rips or tears. The cord’s wattage rating should be greater than the wattage of what you’ve plugged into it.

Sources indicate that to shut down the generator, turn off or disconnect the appliances plugged into it. Then refer to your user’s manual to power down the generator—typically you’ll need to turn the circuit breaker, engine switch, and fuel valve to the “off” position.

Wait until the generator is completely cooled down before storing it once power is restored. If you don’t anticipate needing it again for more than a month, drain the fuel and carburetor. Leaving old fuel can damage the generator’s internal parts. Refer to your owner’s manual for storage instructions.

When running a portable generator, safety is the name of the game. Keep these tips in mind before, during, and after use.

Industry observers note that particulate matter—including tiny airborne particles like pollen, smoke, soot, and other debris—is one of the most common indoor air pollutants, says Dr. Jaspreet Dhau, an expert on indoor air quality and purification and vice president of research and development at Molekule in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida. “Fine particulate matter, particularly PM2.5, which is a particle measuring 2.5 microns [micrometers] or smaller, is a concern because it can travel deep into the respiratory system,” says Dhau. Common sources include cooking, burning candles, using a fireplace, vacuuming, and even opening windows when outdoor pollution levels are high.

Recent findings suggest that VOCs are gases released by certain household products and materials such as paint, solvents, flooring, furniture, adhesives, cleaning supplies, air fresheners, and personal care products. “VOC levels may be higher during and after a home renovation, when fresh furniture is brought into a home, or when products containing chemical ingredients are used without adequate ventilation,” claims Dhau. For example, certain pressed wood furniture and building materials can release formaldehyde, he explains.

Industry observers note that carbon monoxide (CO) is a combustion byproduct, a pollutant released when something burns. “In a typical home, sources can include gas stoves, fireplaces, wood-burning stoves, furnaces, water heaters, candles, and tobacco products,” notes Dhau. “Carbon monoxide is especially dangerous because it’s colorless and odorless, making it difficult to detect without a working CO alarm.”.

Biological contaminants such as dust mites and pet dander are airborne pollutants that originate from living organisms, claims Dhau. “Dust mites are a frequent glitch and tend to collect in mattresses, carpets, upholstered furniture, and bedding. They can enter homes through open windows, pets, clothing, and HVAC systems,” he explains. Signs you might have a problem include frequent dust buildup on surfaces, allergy symptoms, excess pet hair and dander, and dust accumulating around air vents, adds Bill Myers, indoor air quality expert and group manager for technical sales at Panasonic Eco Systems North America.

As conservative Supreme Court Justice Neil Gorsuch recently put it, "Everything is an emergency" now. A recent report by the progressive Brennan Center for Justice similarly warns that "presidents of both parties have stretched the meaning of 'emergency' far beyond reason, enabling them to draw from a growing stockpile of statutory authorities with few real safeguards." Both Gorsuch and the Brennan Center are right.

In his second term, President Donald Trump has engaged in especially grave abuse of emergency powers. But the problem predates his return to power, and is likely to outlast his departure from the political scene. The Democrats' massive victory in the 2026 midterm election gives Congress an opportunity to begin enacting much-needed constraints on executive emergency powers. Some of those authorities should be abolished completely. Others need tighter constraints to ensure they are limited in duration, confined to genuine emergency situations, and subject to strong, nondeferential judicial review enforcing these restrictions.

Industry observers note that some of the powers in question arise from the National Emergencies Act of 1976, which has been particularly prone to abuse. But others involve different legislation, such as the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), the Alien Enemies Act, laws governing domestic use of the military, and various statutes delegating tariff authority to the executive.

According to recent reports, while Trump's abuses of power can provide an initial impetus for reform, there is room for potential cross-ideological cooperation here. Some of the necessary reforms have previously been advocated by conservative Republicans. Federal prosecutors urged jurors Monday to convict Chinese technology firm Huawei, arguing during closing statements in the ongoing 11-week trial involving trade secrets theft and sanctions evasion that the company had grown by repeatedly committing crimes.

According to a Monday story from Law.com, Meredith Arfa, the assistant U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Upcoming York, told jurors that Huawei spent two decades pursuing growth “by any means possible.”.

To illustrate the trade secrets allegations, Arfa played a video of a former Huawei employee removing part of Tappy, T-Mobile’s robot for testing phone touchscreens, from the carrier’s lab. She also highlighted side-by-side images of Cisco’s and Huawei’s router source code, saying the two matched exactly—down to an engineer’s stray comment mentioning someone named “Bob.”.

“This simply couldn’t happen without copying,” Arfa said in her summation.

She further alleged that Huawei managers encouraged theft by paying bonuses for obtaining confidential competitor information, and that employees boasted about it on an internal forum.

In a recent development, on the sanctions compliance allegations, prosecutors said Huawei secretly controlled Skycom, a subsidiary that supplied sensitive technology to Iran’s government. Arfa said the company repeatedly lied about owning Skycom. She also pointed to admissions by Meng Wanzhou, Huawei’s chief financial officer, who signed a deferred prosecution agreement after spending three years under house arrest. Meng acknowledged that Skycom’s operations violated U.S. sanctions, and that she misled HSBC, Huawei’s primary bank, about its compliance, Arfa noted.

Huawei, one of the largest telecommunications companies in the world, denies the allegations, contending that the case rests on the independent actions of rogue employees who were disciplined.

Sources indicate that the government announced the case in 2019. The company is represented by Jenner & Block, Sidley Austin and Steptoe.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, ice melt salt is an effective option for preventing and removing ice from sidewalks, driveways and stairs, but it isn’t suitable for every surface.
  • Sources indicate that ice melt salt chemically reacts with certain materials, accelerates freeze-thaw cycles and alters surface moisture levels to cause damage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Avoid damaging salt-sensitive outdoor surfaces with these expert-backed suggestions.

In a recent development, ice melt salt is an effective option for preventing and removing ice from sidewalks, driveways and stairs, but it isn’t suitable for every surface. Applying ice melt to certain materials can cause significant damage and should be avoided. Ahead, learn which surfaces are most vulnerable to damage from ice melt, why it happens and what safer alternatives you can use to keep outdoor areas free from ice.

Sources indicate that ice melt salt chemically reacts with certain materials, accelerates freeze-thaw cycles and alters surface moisture levels to cause damage. The type of damage will depend on the surface and how it interacts with ice melt.

Ice melt contains rock salt, calcium chloride and/or magnesium chloride to melt ice faster and at lower temperatures. While all melting salt is corrosive and can damage outdoor surfaces, ice melt products can react differently than rock salt alone.

Sources indicate that ice melt seeps deeply into porous cement-based materials. The calcium chloride in ice melt can react with elements of concrete or brick to form calcium oxychloride crystals. As the crystals grow, they generate extreme pressure that can cause cracks, surface spalling and crumbling.

De-icing products accelerate freeze-thaw cycles in porous cement-based surfaces, causing them to break down. “It makes the freezing and thawing cycle more aggressive, which is what causes the surface to break up,” Murphy indicates.

According to recent reports, though less damaging than rock salt, ice melt can still contribute to deterioration. Calcium chloride and magnesium chloride attract and retain moisture, increasing the potential for freeze-thaw damage.

In a recent development, conversely, ice melt draws moisture out of organic materials, causing them to dry out. Over time, this moisture loss can lead to warping, cracking, splitting and other forms of deterioration.

Ice melt accelerates metal oxidation to create rust. It can corrode rebar embedded in concrete, potentially causing cracks and structural damage, as well as rusting exposed metal stairs and railings.

It’s best to avoid applying salt to these salt-sensitive surfaces.

It has been revealed that “Newly introduced concrete is the most vulnerable because it takes weeks to fully cure, so salt on the surface will cause the top few millimeters to flake off,” Murphy says. To be safe, avoid salting new concrete for the first season.

“Cracked concrete opens up for water to get inside, and salt in the water will only make that worse because it will freeze and thaw more aggressively,” Murphy states.

All ice melt products will damage hard-scape surfaces due to chemical reactions and freeze-thaw cycles. “If you are using them, use them sparingly and remove them as soon as possible to decrease continuous exposure for your hardscape areas,” Zurcher states.

Natural stone like limestone and flagstone can react to ice melt compounds. The porous surface is vulnerable to damaging freeze-thaw cycles as well.

Harsh de-icers can damage dyed, painted or stamped concrete surfaces by breaking down color pigments.

Metal stairs and railings will rapidly rust when salt is applied to them, so it’s best to avoid it.

It has been revealed that ice melt draws moisture from wood, causing cracking, warping and raised fibers. It also degrades paint and stain and leaves behind chalky white salt stains.

Sand: Sand doesn’t melt ice, but does provide traction to prevent slips.

Wood ash: Instead of throwing away wood ash, use it as a salt alternative to melt ice and also provide improved traction.

Electric mats: Installed before cold weather sets in, electric melting mats warm up and prevent ice from ever forming. These can be very effective on stairs and sidewalks.

Weed torch: Weed torches are handy when you need to melt a lot of ice quickly. Do not use one to melt ice on wood and avoid painted or stained concrete as well.

Industry observers note that “The best way to reduce damage from these chemicals is to shovel snow as soon as possible,” Zurcher says, so you can use less of them. Use ice melt sparingly, and only as directed. A handful is enough to treat three square yards. Instead of using ice melt alone, mix a small amount with sand to treat surfaces.

Regular sealing protects cement-based products. “Reseal every three to five years to make sure no water can get in, salty or not,” Murphy notes. Additionally, use chloride-free de-icing products, or those labelled as “concrete-safe”.

Newly poured concrete is the most vulnerable to salt damage, but all concrete surfaces will experience damage with enough prolonged exposure to salt.

It has been revealed that it depends on the extent of the damage. Major cracks and breakage mean concrete needs to be removed and repoured, Zurcher indicates, while surface damage could be skim-coated, with potentially limited results.

Pet-safe products will have similar effects on hardscape areas, Zurcher notes, as they still contain salt.

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Power outages are top of mind now more than ever before—and for good reason. One in four households experience a power outage in a year, according to U.S. Census Bureau data, and 70 percent of those reporting outages were without power for 6 hours or more. These longer outages are not only disruptive; they can also be expensive, considering that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration recommends tossing perishable food kept in the refrigerator after just 4 hours without power.

In a recent development, backup power promises comfort and security, which is why so many homes rely on a portable generator or power station. That category has grown from gas-powered generators to multi-fuel units, portable power stations, and whole-home batteries. The newest member of the family? A fridge backup.

Just in 2026, this new style hard-debuted with models from three industry leaders: Bluetti’s Fridge Power, Jackery’s FridgeGuard, and Backup Core by BioLite. And the consumer response has been powerful. Bluetti’s Kickstarter hit 145 percent of its funding goal in 45 days. Jackery debuted as a Costco exclusive in June and expanded its retail distribution after hearing about customers carrying home multiple units. BioLite has released its Backup in two waves already, each selling out in weeks, and is taking orders now for January shipments. Clearly, homeowners want a backup built just for the fridge. Keep reading to learn more about what sets fridge backups apart and when one beats a generator.

Fridge-optimized batteries all share three main hallmarks:.

In a recent development, think of it like a larger version of the uninterruptible power supply (UPS) that you might use in a home office or with a high-end entertainment center to keep your connected electronics running during a brownout or blackout. A UPS in the home office might offer surge protection and enough battery life to run your computer for another 5 minutes so you can safely shut it down; this fridge-optimized backup can keep your most vital kitchen appliance on for 15 hours or more.

And while we call them “fridge” backups, the design is actually much more versatile. Plug them in and slip the slim backups easily into any room to keep an vital appliance operational for hours: under a bed to power a CPAP machine, behind a bookshelf within cord’s reach of an air purifier, or behind the fish tank to maintain the family pet’s habitat.

It has been revealed that kickstarter backers for the Backup by BioLite—which first debuted in 2024 on the crowdfunding platform—“got it” immediately. “They understood the problem it was solving, and most questions revolved around understanding additional applications and setups beyond the fridge because the kitchen application was so intuitive,” says Erica Rosen, the VP of Marketing at BioLite and Goal Zero brands. “For example, we got a lot of questions about sump pumps and if Backup could run one during an outage.” (Spoiler alert: It can.).

Today, homeowners (and renters!) have many options for backup power, each with its own set of pros and cons.

Sources indicate that A standby generator or whole-home battery backup automatically kicks in to keep the essentials—if not the whole home—running during an outage. Each type of backup connects at the electrical panel with a transfer switch. As such, each is a larger investment (read: more expensive) and a permanent installation that requires a licensed electrician. These backups also require forethought about fuel. A standby generator will require a source of liquid propane and/or natural gas, whereas whole-home batteries are often charged from the grid before an event and potentially recharged via solar panels when the grid is down.

Industry observers note that A portable gas-powered generator is more affordable than a standby option, but should only be run outdoors, which creates some limitations. For starters, you need to be home to turn a portable generator on and connect to your appliance. Then, you’ll need a long, heavy-duty outdoor-rated extension cord to reach the kitchen. These generators operate loudly, emit exhaust fumes, and require you to store enough fuel to be ready for the worst. Assuming you have a good supply, though, you can keep your appliance(s) powered with minimal interruption using a reliable portable generator.

A power station brings backup power indoors to power multiple electronics and small appliances. Power stations are the closest comparison. They are safe to use indoors or out and feature similar battery capacities. You can find options in the ballpark of 1 to 2 kWh for similar price points. They can, but may not always be, plugged in 100 percent of the time to act as a UPS. And importantly, they’re often too bulky to leave out next to a refrigerator 24/7.

A fridge backup offers instant power backup without a permanent installation. It’s ideal for the consumer who is looking for a user-friendly, set-and-forget setup and a safety net that offers enough power to keep a fridge running for approximately 15 hours while the power is out—longer if additional batteries are connected.

Sources indicate that “It’s [designed for] someone who wants peace of mind without having to think too much about backup power. Maybe you live somewhere with frequent storms, or you’ve come home after an outage to find everything in your freezer has spoiled,” states Beau Tyrrel, Product Manager at Jackery. “It’s also useful for renters and those who live in apartments and can’t install a whole-home backup system. All you need is a standard outlet, and you can take it with you when you move.”.

According to recent reports, the design is appealing in more ways than one, notes Luna Yan, affiliate marketing manager at Bluetti. A fridge backup solves spatial problems that come with more traditional portable power stations: “Traditional backup power systems are often bulky, making them difficult to accommodate in homes with limited space, particularly in kitchens and apartments.”.

It has been revealed that “When we set out to develop Backup, we knew the world didn’t need another box-format power station. We did a lot of user research and found that there was a meaningful gap between the power stations of the world and expensive whole-home backup solutions, and it was leaving a lot of people out of the resiliency conversation,” Rosen says. “As we explored ways to answer this, it became clear that form factor was going to be a really key element: If we wanted something plugged in permanently to enable automatic performance, it needed to be really easy and it could not take up precious living space.”.

Sources indicate that it’s especially useful if you’re away when the power goes out and can’t move the fridge’s plug to a generator. Already plugged into the wall from setup, the backup’s stored power will be usable immediately. Each model’s mobile app demonstrates outage alerts, battery level, and power draw from anywhere.

“[A fridge backup is] also useful for renters and those who live in apartments and can’t install a whole-home backup system. All you need is a standard outlet, and you can take it with you when you move.”.

There’s a cost to every power outage. One of the biggest concerns for most homeowners is the spoiled food in a refrigerator after 4 hours without power. “Refrigerators are one of the few appliances in your home that needs to run around the clock,” Tyrrel notes. “When the power goes out, you could lose hundreds of dollars in groceries.”.

Sources indicate that A blackout can cost the average American household $117 in spoiled groceries, according to a survey of more than 1,000 Americans by the Texas electric provider Payless Power. One in five homes had it worse, losing more than $200 in groceries during a single outage.

In a recent development, using that average, we estimate that a $1,000 fridge backup pays for itself after 10 blackouts—potentially sooner in larger households or homes with especially packed fridges and freezers. For an area that experiences one to two extended blackouts in a year, this investment could earn its keep in as soon as 6 years—and these upcoming backups are rated for 10 or more years of use.

“Based on customer feedback, refrigerators are among the most important appliances to keep running during a power outage,” Yan indicates. And for good reason: “Continuous refrigeration helps protect food, medications, and other temperature-sensitive items.”.

Recent findings suggest that if your utility company offers a Time-of-Use (TOU) electricity pricing initiative, any of these fridge backups can help you take advantage of the savings. TOU programs charge different supply rates based on when you use electricity, incentivizing customers to use more electricity when overall demand is low by charging less per kilowatt-hour (kWh) used. These “off-peak hours” vary by plan, but typically are overnight and early morning.

In a recent development, for the average homeowner, the main way to save on these looks is to optimize the electricity usage you can schedule: when you charge an electric vehicle, run the dishwasher, and wash or dry a load of laundry. A fridge, of course, runs all day, and an efficient, Energy Star-certified model can use anywhere from 358 kWh for a compact top-freezer unit to 805 kWh per year for a large side-by-side refrigerator. You can’t optimize the always-on appliance without either a whole-home power bank that recharges in an off-peak hour for use during peak times or, now, a fridge backup. In a connected mobile app, customers specify the best times to charge (off-peak hours) and discharge (peak hours), effectively shifting the fridge’s grid use to cheaper hours.

Especially now, with rising concern about grid stability and the increasing frequency of natural disaster events that disrupt power, demand for energy backups is high. Each of these energy brands has sold out and replenished stock at least once already this year. So while you may be eager to set up your home with the first available fridge backup, here’s a comprehensive look at unit specs to help find the model best suited to your space and needs.

According to recent reports, bluetti’s fridge backup offers the largest base capacity—nearly double that of Jackery FridgeGuard, and expandable to 8 kWh (second only to BioLite’s 10.5 kWh). Divide the total cost by the capacity, and you’re paying about $470 per kWh, which is the most backup per dollar. One unit can power the typical modern fridge for 21 to 48 hours, and a maximized setup of FridgePower plus three BlueCell battery packs can power your fridge for 4 days. (Run time, of course, depends on the specific refrigerator’s energy consumption and usage conditions.) That makes the slim design even more impressive—though at 43 pounds, it’s a two-person job to wall-mount.

Sources indicate that the mobile app provides battery levels, outage status, and charging progress, plus a place to choose among four UPS modes: Standard, PV Priority (which prioritizes solar power), TOU (Time-of-Use), and Custom. It even tracks local weather, alerts you when a storm approaches, and switches to fast charging if needed. An optional magnetic display (sold separately) provides at-a-glance information including percentage charged, energy output, and UPS modes—all without opening your phone.

On paper, the Jackery fridge backup appears to be the unit most specialized for fridge use. It offers up to 15 hours of power in the slimmest profile. One outlet (for the fridge) and a single expansion option make it the least flexible of the three—but if the fridge is all you need, it’s a perfect fit. It’s effective, affordable, lasts up to 16 years, and takes only one person to install the lightweight unit on a wall mount (sold separately). It offers surge protection for your most crucial household appliance during voltage spikes and enough power to start the fridge.

Sources indicate that one distinction Jackery has over its competition is a choice between instant backup UPS and a delayed start. “Your refrigerator’s compressor needs a little time to recover,” Tyrrel explains. “When it stops, refrigerant pressure remains high on one side of the system. Restarting too quickly makes the motor work harder and briefly draw several times its normal current. Delayed Start gives the compressor a short pause before restarting, helping avoid unnecessary strain when power flickers on and off.”.

Industry observers note that from the moment an outage occurs, Backup Core automatically powers a refrigerator for 15 to 30 hours. At 29 inches long, it’s 5 to 6 inches longer than all of the other units, but rotating it can fit one atop even a fridge and its slim design should still slip behind the appliance on its vertical wall mount.

Given its size and expansion capabilities, it should come as no surprise that Backup Core also includes the most outlets for electronics. Whereas another model includes one or two ports on the unit, the forward-thinking BioLite design provides its own power strip—that’s three more openings for small kitchen appliances or other electronics to easily connect.

Sources indicate that bioLite’s Backup Core is a 1.5 kWh solution, similar to its sister brand Goal Zero Yeti 1500 (6th generation). “However, Backup can expand in 1.5kWh increments with the ‘Extend’ model, and chain up to 10.5kWh of localized capacity,” Rosen explains. That’s even more than the combined 8kWh capacity of the Yeti Pro 4000 and Yeti Pro Tank 4000. So while Backup Core is the priciest of the three, it’s also the only one that can grow into something close to a whole-home battery. Think of it less as a fridge backup and more as the first piece of a backup system.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Avoid injury with these expert-backed snow shoveling safety tips.

With autumn in full swing, it’s time to start thinking about preparing for the looming winter months. If you live in a snow-prone climate, this means getting out the shovels, salt and snowblower before the first flakes fly. Even if you’re not upcoming to shoveling, it’s worth learning how to do it safely, as injuries can occur at any time.

Recent findings suggest that shoveling may seem simple, but can lead to strains, pulls and cardiac events if not done properly. Ahead, learn expert-backed tips to shovel snow the right (and safe) way with insights from cardiologist Dr. Bradley Serwer.

It has been revealed that the safest way to shovel snow is to push it as much as possible and avoid lifting. If you must lift snow to remove it, bend at the knees and lift with your legs instead of your back.

According to recent reports, “The most crucial tool when preparing to shovel snow is good common sense,” Serwer says. “Dress appropriately and consider the risks of the job at hand.”.

In a recent development, dress in layers that allow you to remove or open up a layer of clothing as you warm up to avoid getting overheated. Opt for a moisture wicking base layer, a mid-weight layer and a jacket that is wind-resistant and waterproof. Wear warm, waterproof gloves, a hat, warm socks and thick-soled winter boots. For particularly cold temperatures and high winds, add ski goggles and a balaclava to protect sensitive facial skin.

In a recent development, consider a quick warm up and stretch session for a safer shoveling session. Get your blood pumping with some light activity like jumping jacks, walking in place or climbing up and down the stairs in your home. Gently stretch major muscle groups before heading outside.

Industry observers note that snow shovels are not all created equal. For safer shoveling, choose one that is less demanding on your back, joints and heart. Ergonomic shovels feature a curved handle that reduces back strain when lifting. Snow plow shovels are meant to push snow only, not lift it. And battery-powered shovels act like mini-snowblowers to quickly remove snow without any manual input.

It has been revealed that keep your back straight, bend at the knees and use your legs to lift snow for safer shoveling. Keep the loaded shovel close to your body, then, without twisting, turn your body toward the direction you place the snow. If snow is wet or deeper than six inches, remove it in smaller layers, rather than one heavy shovelful.

Recent findings suggest that “It is often underestimated what kind of physical workload is required to shovel a substantial amount of snow,” Serwer notes. That’s why it’s important to pace yourself, stop regularly and plan ahead to avoid overexertion. Opt for a slow and steady pace, especially if you’re typically sedentary. Rigorous snow shoveling will quickly lead to overexertion and cardiac strain. Going slow allows you to focus on safe shoveling technique, preventing possible muscle strains and pulls. Stay well-hydrated when shoveling and take regular breaks to allow your heart rate to return to normal and your muscles to recover.

Stop shoveling if you’re experiencing cardiac distress, cold-related conditions, dehydration or back strain.

It has been revealed that “Shoveling snow can be a very strenuous activity, placing notable strain on the cardiovascular system,” Serwer indicates. Know the signs of a heart attack before picking up a shovel, like chest pressure, shortness of breath, nausea and radiating arm pain. Stop immediately if you experience these symptoms and seek medical help. “Hire someone else to shovel, especially if you are at a high cardiac risk,” Serwer says.

Dress in layers and cover exposed skin in freezing temperatures and wind. Even with these efforts, frostbite and hypothermia are real risks. Frostbite begins in extremities like fingers and toes, and exposed facial skin. Early signs include pale, cold skin and prickling or numb sensations. Hypothermia happens when core body temperatures drop too low and begins with clumsiness, foggy thinking, fatigue and intense shivering. Stop immediately and go inside to warm up if you experience these symptoms.

“It is very easy to become dehydrated while working in cold climates,” Serwer says, as the human body suppresses the thirst response and dry winter air pulls additional moisture from our bodies. Notice signs of dehydration like fatigue, dry throat, cracked lips or a headache. “Dehydration is often overlooked, and people don’t replace the fluids as needed,” Serwer adds. Stop and take regular water breaks and continue drinking fluids for the remainder of the day if you notice these signs.

According to recent reports, shoveling puts strain on your spine and back, and can lead to serious, long term injuries like herniated disks, sciatica and lower back strains if you’re not careful. Beyond always lifting with your legs, stop shoveling if you feel the early signs of spine and back strain. These include a dull, aching in your lower back, sharp pain when bending or twisting, muscle cramping or shooting pains.

It is safer to push snow rather than lift it.

It has been revealed that individuals with heart disease, obesity, diabetes and high blood pressure should not shovel snow. Those over 45 years old should also exercise caution.

It has been revealed that we selected and tested a diverse assortment of waterproof gloves designed for a variety of uses in different seasons. For all of them, our key testing consideration was whether the gloves were truly waterproof. To find out, we used three testing methods and allowed the gloves to thoroughly dry between tests. All comments about sizing are subjective, based on sizing guides provided by the manufacturers and perceived comfort by the tester. On those gloves not listed as unisex, women tested women’s gloves, and men tested men’s gloves.

First, we simulated storm conditions with a rain-wand attachment on a garden hose. The testers wore each pair of gloves beneath a steady 2-minute shower, flexing their hands and turning them over to expose all parts of the gloves to the stream. In the second test, we immersed our gloved hands into a bucket of water, again flexing and rotating to ensure that they were completely wet. Finally, we tested them for wet-gripping ability while handling smooth wet stones. To merit inclusion in this guide, each pair of gloves passed all three tests with minimal water intrusion to the inside of the glove.

Before shopping for the best waterproof gloves, consider the type of work planned for the gloves as well as the kind of materials and construction desired. In this section, we review some key considerations to keep in mind while shopping for the best waterproof gloves, including materials, use, fit, and more.

According to recent reports, choosing the best waterproof gloves depends on how they’ll be used. Work gloves are completely different from those intended for outdoor sports or casual wear.

In a recent development, on garments labeled “waterproof,” the outer shell is usually where the magic happens. Materials like tightly woven nylon, polyester, softshell technical materials, treated leather, and others work well to shed water before it can seep through to the lining. Keep in mind that it’s very rare for leather gloves to actually be waterproof; more likely, they are simply water-resistant.

Aside from shell material, other elements in waterproof gloves’ exteriors make them useful in wet or messy situations. Some of the best waterproof gloves, for example, have textured grips that make it easier for the wearer to grab on to wet, slippery surfaces, making them ideal for skiing, cycling, and other active pursuits. Those looking for waterproof gloves for work may want to invest in gloves with reinforced palms and thumbs, which should last longer and stand up to more wear.

The best waterproof gloves contain an optional outer shell with conductors that transfer the electrical charge from a finger to a touch screen, allowing consumers to manipulate their phones without removing their gloves.

Sources indicate that some of the best waterproof gloves contain insulation that captures body heat, which forms air pockets that warm with the heat from the hand. Most insulation is a man-made poly-fill material such as Thinsulate or 3M.

According to recent reports, to ensure gloves keep warm air inside and cold air from seeping in, some waterproof gloves have long elastic cuffs that hug tight to the wrist and arm, closing off any pathway for air to enter. For even warmer gloves, look for removable liners that can slip inside a waterproof glove to add another layer of insulation.

When selecting the best waterproof gloves, fit and comfort are essential. However, a “good fit” is relative to the activity. A pair of running gloves fits quite differently than a pair of winter work gloves or ski gloves.

Waterproof running or hiking gloves often feel like a stretchy, flexible second skin. Because they’re lightweight and wick away moisture, people sometimes forget they’re even wearing them.

It has been revealed that waterproof work gloves are bulkier and a bit stiff because they’re generally made from thick nylon or leather that resists ripping, tearing, and friction. Moreover, extra padding or reinforcement on the thumbs or palms can add to their bulk. Though work gloves fit loosely, they shouldn’t be so loose that it’s difficult to pick up small items while wearing them.

Sources indicate that ski gloves are flexible but don’t wear particularly well because they’re typically made from materials like nylon. Properly fitting ski gloves fit snugly around the wrist but are roomy enough to allow the skier to manipulate straps on ski poles and boot bindings.

Also consider breathability. If hands sweat and moisture collects inside the glove, it won’t matter that the shell is waterproof because hands will still get wet. Breathable gloves help some of the heat and moisture escape without letting in cold outer air and moisture.

Now that you know a bit more about the factors to consider when choosing the best waterproof gloves for your needs, some questions may remain. The following are some of the most frequently asked questions about the best waterproof gloves, so check for an answer to your question below.

According to recent reports, waterproof means that absolutely no water makes its way into the glove. Water-resistant means that the gloves shed water to a degree before water comes in.

As one of the best options for the warmest waterproof gloves, the Carhartt Cold Snap waterproof gloves are warm enough to protect your hands in very cold temperatures.

You can wash some waterproof gloves, but it’s best to spot clean them and use a boot dryer with a glove attachment if they become soiled.

The best way to dry the inside of waterproof gloves is to put them on a boot dryer with a glove attachment.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that from Judge Norman Moon (W.D.
  • The University of Virginia's ("UVA") Post-Baccalaureate Pre-Medical Program is a one-year curriculum designed for pre-med students who did not complete all prerequisites during their undergraduate study….
  • It has been revealed that plaintiff … did exceptionally well [in the Program], earning a "near-perfect" GPA and a 96th-percentile score on the Medical College Admission Test ….
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that from Judge Norman Moon (W.D. Va.) Wednesday in Smith v. Rector & Visitors of Univ. of Va.:.

The University of Virginia's ("UVA") Post-Baccalaureate Pre-Medical Program is a one-year curriculum designed for pre-med students who did not complete all prerequisites during their undergraduate study…. The Program … boasts a 94% medical-school placement rate and, accordingly, is highly selective ….

It has been revealed that plaintiff … did exceptionally well [in the Program], earning a "near-perfect" GPA and a 96th-percentile score on the Medical College Admission Test …. [After finishing the Program,] Plaintiff applied to thirty medical schools …. Plaintiff asked the [Post-Baccalaureate Pre-Medical Program Committee] for a letter of recommendation. These "Committee Letters" reflect "the Program's collective institutional assessment of the applicant," scaled on a score of 1 (unable to recommend at this time) to 5 (recommended with enthusiasm)….

Sources indicate that plaintiff alleges that he received "highly favorable" letters from his individual recommenders, who praised his intellect, work ethic, personality, and overall potential to succeed in medical school. In contrast to these letters, however, the Committee allegedly wrote a "materially adverse" letter and assigned Plaintiff a score of 2 (recommended with reservations)….

Plaintiff was rejected by all thirty medical schools he applied to, twenty-eight rejecting him without an interview. Given his otherwise strong qualifications, Plaintiff identifies the Committee letter as the clear explanation for this failure. But not only did the letter devastate these thirty applications, Plaintiff maintains—it also "derail[ed] his entire future and eradicate[ed] his chances of pursuing a career in medicine." ….

Plaintiff sued for, among other things, defamation, based on these statements from the Committee Letter:.

The court held that "Statements 1, 4, and 5 are pure expressions of opinion":.

The operative parts of these statements are that Plaintiff, relative to other students, was immature, awkward, and had occasional difficulty following class conversation. It is indeed true, as Plaintiff points out, that the Committee's assessments differ from those of his professors in their individual letters of recommendation. But that only suggests a difference of opinion between the professors and the Committee.

One person, endowed with the gift of gab, might believe an individual to be a poor conversationalist, while another person, more maladroit in nature, might believe that same individual to be perfectly charming. Likewise, someone with a particularly high standard for maturity might conclude that someone is immature where most others would disagree. This is to say that the Statements 1, 4, and 5 are "relative in nature and depend largely upon the [Defendants'] viewpoint." {To the extent that Plaintiff alleges that his level 2 "recommended with reservations" rating was itself defamatory, the Court finds that it is also a pure expression of opinion.}.

The court concluded that statements 2 and 3 included factual implications, and thus weren't pure opinion:.

It is impossible to separate the negative import of each statement from the assumptions that Plaintiff, in fact, did not "keep[ ] his shadowing assignments" and did not "communicat[e] his intended class absences" at least once, as even a single instance of either might reasonably fail to meet expectations in a "highly selective" program. These assumptions, moreover, are susceptible to empirical proof. That the Committee Letter ultimately phrases each statement as a relative assessment does not negate that, if the factual predicates are false, then the assessment must also be false.

But the court concluded that statement 3 was true, since Plaintiff had "acknowledg[ed] three unexcused absences in a class." And it also concluded that statements 2 and 3 weren't sufficiently damaging to reputation to be defamatory:.

Statements that are merely "insulting, offensive, or otherwise inappropriate" are not defamatory. The bar is much higher: "Reputation must be affected to a magnitude sufficient to render one odious, infamous, or ridiculous, or subject to disgrace, shame, scorn, or contempt.".

Therefore, and relevant here, negative assessments of a person's professional conduct are rarely defamatory unless they suggest "an unfitness to perform the duties of a job or lack of integrity in the performance of duties." … "[A]llegations of unsatisfactory job performance do not in and of themselves so harm [one's] reputation …." ….

Statements 2 and 3 do not plausibly rise to this level. The purpose of the Committee Letter was to "convey[ ] UVA's institutional assessment of Plaintiff's readiness and suitability for medical school," and its general tenor was that Plaintiff possesses the raw intellectual capability but would first "benefit from some maturing years," reflected in its recommendation "with reservations." To concretize the Committee's "reservations," the letter stated that Plaintiff "was not as consistent with keeping his shadowing assignments or communicating his intended class absences as expected.".

These statements criticize Plaintiff's communication and consistency regarding his attendance—they do not, for instance, suggest that he was chronically absent or that he abandoned his clinical duties. See, e.g., Fuste v. Riverside Healthcare Ass'n, Inc. (Va. 2003) (a statement suggesting two doctors "'abandoned' their patients and that there were 'concerns about their competence'" was defamatory per se); Fleming v. Moore (Va. 1981) (requiring that a statement be "necessarily hurtful" to a plaintiff's occupational fitness to be defamatory per se). Moreover, and as Plaintiff recognizes, these statements were not offered to suggest that he was wholly unsuited for medical school—they were offered in support of his assessment as capable yet not presently ready for medical school. See Dkt. 32 at 20 ("[The Committee Letter] conveyed that Plaintiff presently lacked the maturity, judgment, and readiness required to enter medical school."); id. ("Read in that context, the Committee was telling medical schools that Plaintiff was not yet fit to begin medical training and should not be admitted during the current application cycle."). While this assessment may have harmed Plaintiff's candidacy in the 2025 application cycle, it did not malign his reputation as to render him "odious, infamous, or ridiculous" or subject him to "disgrace, shame, scorn, or contempt.".

Charles Walker Terry and Samantha Rosalie Romano (Byrne Canaan Law) represent defendants.

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Recent findings suggest that imagine your frustration when your driveway is covered in snow after the first winter storm, but your snow blower won’t start. As winter approaches, it’s time to make sure your snow blower is ready to tackle that first snowfall. You’ll want to take a few steps to check that it’s tuned up and ready to go without a hitch. We spoke to Sean Dwyer, senior product manager for commercial and residential wheeled products at Husqvarna Group North America to identify the top snow blower maintenance tasks to prioritize so you are prepared when the first snowflake falls.

By far the most notable step is to make sure you have a fresh supply of fuel, states Dwyer. “If you have regular pump fuel, it should be less than 30 days old, and ideally premium grade that’s a non-ethanol blend,” he explains. Fuel can go stale over time and gum up the snow blower’s carburetor. Dwyer recommends running the unit out of gas before storing it. “Otherwise, at a minimum, purchase stabilized canned fuel or add a fuel stabilizer.” Gasoline with a stabilizer typically lasts for about 4 to 6 months.

It has been revealed that spend some time reviewing the key components of the unit. “This means checking engine oil and tire pressures, and also starting the unit to ensure proper wheel drive and auger operation,” notes Dwyer. “This is also a good time to shut the fuel off and run the carburetor dry to give your snow blower the best chance of a successful operation when you need it.”.

In addition, pay attention to these additional parts of the snow blower:.

Featuring an easy-to-pour package and effective formula, this motor oil washes dirt and deposits out of the engine as it passes through.

Battery-powered snow blowers are convenient, but it’s crucial to recognize that cold weather and batteries don’t typically work well together, warns Dwyer. Checking battery health is part of regular snow blower maintenance. Rechargeable batteries can degrade over time, and won’t be able to hold as much charge as they age as they do when new. He recommends keeping fully charged batteries in the house or a location where they will remain above freezing temperatures. “If everything is in the cold garage, there is a good chance they won’t work when you need them to,” he explains. “Also, remember that when you are done, bring the batteries back to a warm place so they are ready to go next time.”.

Snow blowers typically contain shear bolts (also called pins) as a safety feature. The shear bolts are designed to break to protect the auger gears from damage if the unit runs into hard objects like ice from a blizzard. There is typically one pin on each auger and one or two on the impeller.

In a recent development, to change these components, wear protective gloves. “With the engine shut off, try to rotate each individual auger by hand,” claims Dwyer. “You should not be able to rotate the augers, and the shear bolts will be visually present.” To check the impeller, look for the shear bolts, or hold one of the augers firmly, and slowly try to turn the impeller. “Be careful when checking the impeller, as it is tied to the shaft that will drive the augers.”.

If these items spin freely, the shear bolt is likely damaged or missing, says Dwyer. Replace any missing or broken bolts to protect your snow blower. It’s a good idea to always keep a stash of shear bolts on hand.

Recent findings suggest that designed to wear down with use, skid shoes help keep a snow blower’s housing at the correct height and also protect your pavement. They are located on the lower sides of the auger housing and are designed to hold the scraper, located at the bottom of the auger housing, just above the ground, states Dwyer. “As these shoes wear, the scraper will contact the ground and wear will increase,” he explains.

“A simple way to adjust the shoes is to sit the snow blower scraper on something around ¼ inch thick, like a paint stir stick, and then loosen the bolts holding the shoes to adjust them down to contact the ground and retighten,” suggests Dwyer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Those roadside scales do more than weigh semitrucks. Here’s what inspectors check and what happens when a truck pulls into a weigh station.

Sources indicate that drivers pass truck weigh stations all the time, but few know everything these stations do or what happens when a truck pulls in. Once a semitruck exits and rejoins the highway, it’s hard to tell what goes on in between.

Learn what happens when a truck pulls in, what inspectors look for, and why some drivers can keep going.

Truck weigh stations help states enforce weight limits and spot safety problems. Trucks can weigh too much overall or carry too much weight on certain axles, putting extra strain on roads and bridges. On the Interstate System, the standard federal limits are 80,000 pounds gross vehicle weight, 20,000 pounds on a single axle, and 34,000 pounds on a tandem axle. Federal bridge weight rules and certain exceptions can also affect how much a truck may legally carry. Limits on other roads can vary.

Rules vary by state. “Some require all commercial motor vehicles to stop, while others require only those above a certain weight to stop,” according to the Federal Highway Administration. “Ultimately, States must certify that they are enforcing their weight limits on certain highways in order not to jeopardize their receipt of Federal highway funds.”.

According to recent reports, drivers who pull in follow signs directing them to a scale, where their trucks are weighed either while moving slowly or at a complete stop. If the weight is within the limits, they may be cleared to leave. Inspectors may still pull a truck aside for a closer look even when its weight is fine, based on screening results, visible defects, or random selection. An overweight truck may also be inspected further.

Sources indicate that inspectors may check a truck’s tires, brakes, lights, and cargo, along with the driver’s records. They may also review credentials and permits, such as registration and fuel-tax paperwork, along with the driver’s hours-of-service logs. “There are eight levels of inspections ranging from the Level I Inspection, which evaluates both the driver and vehicle, to inspection levels with a more specific area of focus, such as Level VI for radioactive materials and Level VIII for electronic inspections,” according to the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance.

Drivers of overweight trucks may receive a citation or have to move or remove some cargo before leaving. The exact consequences vary by state and violation.

Industry observers note that more serious safety problems, like faulty brakes, can put a truck or driver out of service. A truck placed out of service can’t return to the road until the problem is fixed. Drivers placed out of service must wait until their restrictions end.

Some trucks can skip the stop altogether through electronic bypass programs. These programs use safety records and other information to determine whether a driver can continue without entering the station. Drivers still have to follow any signs or signals telling them to stop.

NBA superstar LeBron James is suing the makers of sports betting app Bron, claiming that it is intentionally ripping off his nickname.

Sources indicate that in a federal complaint filed Tuesday in the Southern District of Latest York, James stated he has been known as “Bron” since he was a young basketball standout in Ohio. He alleges that PlayVision and its co-founders, Anish Gupta and Marc Zoghby, seek “to trade on” his “valuable name and reputation” by naming their app Bron.

In a recent development, there is no other connection between the word and the defendants or any other feature of their app, James alleges. He also argues in the complaint that when the defendants launched a marketing campaign for the Bron app earlier this month, they used a video advertisement that incorporated an artificial intelligence-generated version of him.

According to recent reports, “The AI-generated version of Mr. James sits in an NBA-style locker room wearing a basketball jersey bearing Mr. James’s nickname, ‘Bron,’ above the number ‘23’—a number associated with Mr. James and the one he currently wears on the Philadelphia 76ers—with physical traits that mimic Mr. James, down to his identifiable tattoos,” according to the complaint.

“Speaking in Mr. James’s voice, the AI-generated Mr. James scrolls through wagers on other NBA players in defendants’ Bron app,” the complaint continues. “The ad then urges viewers to ‘scroll to bet.’”.

The lawsuit seeks damages and an injunction preventing the defendants from using the “Bron” name; James’ name, image and likeness; and voice.

Courthouse News Service has additional reporting.

A representative for Bron did not respond to the publication’s request for comment.

Sullivan states that the First Amendment "prohibits a public official's recovering damages for a defamatory falsehood relating to his official conduct unless he proves that the statement was made with 'actual malice'—that is, with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not." … {[N]otwithstanding the ordinary meaning and usage of "actual malice," "allegations of ill-will, improper motive or personal animosity play no role in determining whether a defendant acted with actual malice," which "does not concern ill-will, improper motive, or personal animosity," a conclusion which appears correct, in law if not elsewhere in the English language or in the common understanding. In sum, "actual malice is not about whether the speaker had evil intent or a motive arising from ill-will."} "[F]ailure to investigate before publishing, even when a reasonably prudent person would have done so, is not sufficient to establish reckless disregard[.]" Harte-Hanks Communications v. Connaughton (1989).

[But] "reckless disregard may be found where there are obvious reasons to doubt the veracity of the informant or the accuracy of his report." "Although failure to investigate will not alone support a finding of actual malice, the purposeful avoidance of the truth is in a different category." ….

The court concluded that a large set of statements that Trump alleges to be libelous aren't actionable, "for one or more of the many and varied reasons amply and ably explained by the defendants in the motion to dismiss." As described in the complaint, the second article includes the statement (7) "Federal, state and local authorities looked into his ties with the Mafia, found violations of money laundering rules and penalized him for skirting stock trade rules.".

In these seven instances, the allegations of the complaint quite plausibly and reasonably create an inference that the authors and the publishers knew that these statements, accusing the plaintiff of planning and perpetrating complex crimes and knowingly receiving the proceeds and other benefits of these crimes, were "based on incomplete, minimal information" and that the author and the publisher "realized that a responsible assessment of the Trump family's compliance with tax laws would have required forensic auditing, expert tax and legal advice, and other expensive investigatory tools." In other words, the facts alleged in the complaint create at least a plausible inference that the authors and the publishers knew that no reliable conclusion about violations of the tax laws, including especially the estate and gift tax laws, is possible without reliance on qualified opinion formulated after the necessary factual and legal research and analysis, which they knowingly failed to obtain.

The confident detection of tax and other crimes, including money laundering, of the kind that some of the challenged statements attribute to the plaintiff, that is, tax crimes including estate and gift tax crimes and the like, is a task that is intensely fact-dependent, and the law that governs is singularly complex and within the immediate competence of only a relatively small cohort of specialized practitioners.

It has been revealed that anyone who publishes the claim that someone else has committed a crime of the complex nature described in some of the challenged statements and who has not received an explicit opinion from a qualified source after a thorough examination of pertinent facts necessarily proceeds with particularized reason to doubt the truth of their statements and with knowledge of a high degree of probable falsity of the statements; in other words, they know that they don't know, but they are undeterred. Sullivan….

The eastern facade of the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School in 2006. (Photo by Jeffrey M. Vinocur, CC-BY-SA-3.0, via Wikimedia Commons).

Industry observers note that the case of a suspended professor at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School who claims that she was fired because of her race after making comments about minority groups would be better considered as a free speech matter, a panel of the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Philadelphia said Tuesday.

The three-judge panel in Philadelphia suggested that professor Amy Wax’s claims of retaliation for speaking about racial issues was more of a First Amendment issue, rather than employment discrimination, as she had argued.

In her brief, Wax, a white Jewish woman, stated that Title VI of the Civil Rights Act and Section 1981 of the Civil Rights Act prohibit discrimination “on the ground of race” and “on the basis of race,” respectively, differing them from Title VII.

She argued that the the University of Pennsylvania had an alleged double standard, allowing faculty and students to participate in what she called antisemitic demonstrations against Israel without consequences but punishing her for her commentary on race.

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

GTA6 let's you take a break from a life of crime to make some much-needed home repairs on Jason and Lucia's house.

Sources indicate that just in case your algorithm is different from mine, here’s some news: Grand Theft Auto 6 officially released today. After 13 years of waiting, fans of the open-world action-adventure video game series can finally dive into a latest, richly detailed and fully realized virtual world. Boot up the game, and you’ll find yourself faced with surprising realism, a world of crime, and the ability to do just about whatever you want. That’s right, even… DIY home improvement jobs?

Sources indicate that yep, you’re reading that right. As part of its commitment to realism, GTA developer Rockstar Games has given players the ability to do some honest-to-goodness, roll-up-your-sleeves-and-get-to-work home improvement virtually.

In a recent development, and it’s not just a short cutscene where you see the house magically go from disrepair to fully fixed up. You, as the player, have to actually do the work, whether you’re drywalling, painting, or roofing. Luckily, it’s just a video game because the game is also set in a fictional version of Florida in the summer, which is probably one of the last places on earth you’d want to be stuck doing any sort of construction work.

Let’s take a look at a few of the home improvement jobs done by GTA6‘s Jason Duval and see if his work meets Family Handyman’s standards.

In a recent development, with his lady friend Lucia on the way back from prison, Jason decides to fix up the place… including the unfinished framing in the center of his living room. Luckily, Jason knows how to hang drywall. The gameplay represents the job pretty accurately— Jason holds the drywall in place and screws it into the studs with an impact driver. We don’t get to see any taping or mudding, though. 7/10.

Next, we’ll inspect whether Jason should perhaps prioritize a career as a painter over his life of crime. The painting section is also pretty accurate to the average DIY painting experience. Jason has to choose between three different color options before pouring the paint into a tray and using a roller to paint the wall. It’s pretty boring, which is honestly just like painting in real life — so bonus points for immersive realism. 8/10.

One of the first things Jason knows he has to fix before Lucia arrives is the massive hole in his roof that’s letting in a near-constant drip of rain. Luckily, like a lot of DIYers, he has some roofing experience, a cordless nail gun and a stack of shingles just lying around for some reason. Again, this section is pretty realistic. If gamers want the full Florida roofing experience, though, they’ll have to crank their heaters to maximum or perhaps play the game in a sauna. 6/10.

Sources indicate that look, I get it. The Grand Theft Auto series is about living out fantasies, providing gamers a sandbox where they can virtually experience the impossible.

But still… “House repairs complete” is a bridge too far. Ask any DIYer, and they will tell you no house is ever fully repaired. Pretending home improvement work could ever be finished is just not realistic and really took me out of the experience. 3/10.

Industry observers note that overall, the game is cool. But to be honest, I’m not sure what the point is now that the house repairs are complete.

As it gets closer to the most magical time of the year, stores are stocked with decorations big and small, and figuring out how you want your home to look can be a little overwhelming. Thankfully, experts in the home decor space are sharing their seasonal tips to help you get ready.

HGTV’s Jonathan Scott shared a video with a few Christmas decorating hacks he and his partner, Zooey Deschanel, use in their home.

“I like it to be a little bit nostalgic, a little bit fun, and a whole lot of holiday spirit,” Scott says.

Industry observers note that there’s no one right way to decorate for Christmas, and even if so that doesn’t mean you should stick to the conventional script, according to Scott. “There are lots of different rules when decorating for the holidays, but of course, as we know, rules are meant to be broken,” Scott states. “So it really depends on your comfort level.”.

Here are some of Scott’s hacks:.

Even the nicest artificial trees can look a little too perfect. Scott’s trick is to stuff a few extra branches into the tree, leaving some sticking out at random. He also adds more lights, including larger bulbs, even though his tree is already pre-lit.

Recent findings suggest that scott has been collecting nutcrackers for years, and yes, he even names them. Rather than display them the same way every Christmas, he changes things up with different garlands, beads, and branches. It’s a way to get a newly introduced look out of decorations he already owns.

Those giant stacked presents in Scott’s house look like they’d be a pain to store, but they’re not. Each box fits inside the next, so the whole display takes up a fraction of the space once Christmas is over.

You can watch the full video and get more tips here:.

At the top of everyone’s mind around the holidays should be safety.

Scott recommends being mindful of fragile decorations, especially if you have young children or large pets. Glass ornaments and other breakable decorations can easily get knocked over, so consider using sturdier pieces in areas where kids and pets spend a lot of time.

The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) also recommends looking for a “fire resistant” label when purchasing an artificial Christmas tree and regularly watering live trees to reduce fire risks.

Whether you’re adding a few newly introduced touches to your favorite decorations or going all out with a Christmas tree in every room, the most crucial thing is creating a space that feels festive to you.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that from Chief Judge James Boasberg (D.C.C.) today in Doe v. Trump:.

In a recent development, plaintiff Michael Doe is an American citizen whose wife and daughter reside in Kyiv, Ukraine. In March 2025, his wife and daughter were almost killed in a drone strike. On behalf of himself and a class of Ukrainian refugees, Doe sues President Trump, Secretary Rubio, and Elon Musk for violating, inter alia, a federal statute that imposes sanctions on Russia, the Take Care Clause, and the First Amendment. [The claims are apparently related to the Trump Administration's actions related to sanctions on Russia Musk's actions related to Ukraine and Starlink. -EV].

Generally, a complaint must identify the plaintiffs. That requirement reflects the "presumption in favor of disclosure [of litigants' identities], which stems from the 'general public interest in the openness of governmental processes,' and, more specifically, from the tradition of open judicial proceedings." A party moving to proceed pseudonymously thus "bears the weighty burden of both demonstrating a concrete need for such secrecy[] and identifying the consequences that would likely befall it if forced to proceed in its own name." ….

Plaintiff has not established that his interest in pseudonymity outweighs the public's interest in learning his identity….

Recent findings suggest that the Court does not doubt that individuals in Kyiv face brutal, life-threatening dangers, nor does it take their—or their families'—concerns about safety lightly. Plaintiff has failed, however, to link those legitimate fears to his being publicly named in this lawsuit. He provides no evidence that Russia's extensive bombing campaign targets the family members of individuals engaged in Russian-sanction-related lawsuits in the United States. At most, he asserts that "[t]he Russian government have a proven documented history and pattern of targeting anyone, anywhere in the world, who challenges their authority of government," including "documented attempted assassinations" and "the use of sophisticated hacking groups to steal identities, digital assets[,] and to launch drone bombing attacks inside Ukraine.".

In a recent development, doe's broad assertion that Russian retaliates against critics does not establish that it will assassinate him, steal his identity or digital assets, or launch drone strikes at his family members in Ukraine in response to a lawsuit. Absent any specific threats or evidence that his family members will be so targeted, this factor weighs against pseudonymity….

    Recent findings suggest that western civilization is facing a crisis driven by mass immigration from the Muslim world. Across the Atlantic, the demographic consequences of Muslim immigration have begun to unravel the social fabric of Europe. America is following a similar course as its foreign-born population reaches historic levels. Coinciding with this trend, immigration from the Muslim world has increased dramatically in recent decades. After the Hart–Celler Act opened the United States to large-scale immigration from outside Europe in 1965, America’s Muslim diaspora has grown from roughly 100,000 in 1961 to more than 5.5 million today.[REF] Meanwhile, America’s Muslim population has more than doubled since the start of the Global War on Terrorism. If these patterns persist unchecked, they threaten to “change and corrupt the national spirit” of America.[REF]The growing prevalence of Islamic culture presents a host of practical problems for American society. Although Islamification is not yet a national threat on the scale seen in Europe, select urban centers and rural communities have started to become transformed by the influx of unassimilated Muslim immigrants. The West’s Muslim diaspora has demonstrated a striking aversion to assimilation. The case of Lewiston, Maine, where a wave of Somali immigrants has overwhelmed the city since the early 2000s, illustrates the problem. According to Lauren Gilbert, many of the Somali diaspora in Lewiston do not wish to assimilate into America’s “majority culture.” “Many Somali elders,” she reports from interviews, “view assimilation into the American mosaic as a threat to the very survival of the Somali people.” Accordingly, the Somali elders chose Lewiston, in part, “because they believed that they could raise their children and practice their religion in relative peace, free from unwanted outside influences.”[REF]Examples such as Lewiston’s Somali diaspora underscore how America’s embrace of multiculturalism has made it impossible to accommodate Islam without altering the character of the nation itself. As Gilbert acknowledges, “from a multiculturalist perspective, the desire not to assimilate and thus to lose one’s cultural and religious identity is a legitimate choice that the host society should respect and accommodate.”[REF] Many Muslim immigrants and their children reject the traditional “melting pot” settlement that integrated previous waves of immigrants into a unified American national identity.A 2026 op-ed in The Washington Post by Shadi Hamid, a senior fellow at Georgetown University, exemplifies this view. Hamid argues against the premise that “a minority community’s right to be in the United States depends on its willingness to converge with the cultural mainstream.”[REF] In Hamid’s view, “America was not founded on the assumption that its citizens would eventually come to agree on foundational questions.”This sentiment is widely shared by prominent Islamic organizations across America. The Council on American-Islamic Relations’ (CAIR’s) 2026 Civil Rights Report explicitly criticizes the old American tradition on immigration that sought to “preserve the ideal of U.S. homogeneity” and all attempts to restore the vision of America as united by a “single heritage.”[REF] To this end, the report asserts CAIR’s commitment to protecting Muslims’ “right to be different.” A 2009 article reposted by CAIR, which includes “assimilation” in a list of terms “not to use with Muslims,” is further indicative of this prevailing sentiment.[REF] In this same spirit, the Islamic Circle of North America declared in a statement issued ahead of the 25th anniversary of 9/11 that they “reject the premise that American belonging is contingent on loyalty tests or displays of patriotism.”[REF]Contrary to Hamid’s supposition, the Western tradition has long maintained that a republic depends, as Cicero would say, upon a fundamental agreement on justice and the common good. Mass immigration from civilizations with radically different political theologies and conceptions of justice, whose adherents refuse to adopt American cultural mores and the American tradition of ordered liberty, threatens the very existence of that tradition.The old tradition on immigration was rooted in the conviction that “America must be kept American.”[REF] That tradition recognized that too much immigration that is too disparate in culture, religion, and mores would change America’s regime of natural rights, self-government, and ordered liberty into something both foreign and undesirable. On this basis, the Founders would have viewed mass immigration from the Muslim world, and elsewhere, as a threat to both the country’s political and cultural heritage.The Naturalization Acts of the Early Republic, which largely prohibited naturalization of immigrants from outside the Western world, epitomized this consensus. This precedent was subsequently affirmed by the Reconstruction Congress and by several decades of judicial precedents from the early 20th century. Together, these various writings, debates, speeches, statutes, and court opinions form a consistent political tradition that endured for 175 years, beginning with the Naturalization Act of 1790 until the passage of Hart–Celler in 1965. Restoring this tradition offers the surest guide for navigating the challenges posed by mass immigration. What follows is a reconstruction of this tradition’s prevailing ethos.The Founders on Immigration and Republican CitizenshipThe Founding Fathers did not directly address the question of Muslim immigration or the compatibility of the Islamic faith with American society. The dilemmas of late modernity, in many respects, are unique in the history of the nation. As a result, modern Americans cannot simply look back to the Founding generation for a manual on how to solve the crisis of this age. Nevertheless, the Founders thought deeply about the fundamental principles pertaining to those questions—the nature of citizenship in a republic, the moral conditions of freedom, and the need to preserve a common national sentiment. These general principles provide a star and compass for navigating the challenges posed by mass immigration from both the Islamic world and elsewhere.Immigration raises vital questions for political life. A political community, Aristotle writes, “does not arise from any chance multitude” of individuals.[REF] The character of any given political regime depends on the character of its people. If that character changes, the very nature of the regime will change along with it. Aristotle thus warns that a “dissimilarity of stock” caused by an influx of foreigners facilitates regime change by introducing competing and often irreconcilable interests and notions of justice. The Founders likewise worried that indiscriminate immigration would threaten the stability of the republic by undermining national solidarity and transforming American society into “a heterogeneous, incoherent, distracted mass.”[REF]The Founders worried that indiscriminate immigration would threaten the stability of the republic by undermining national solidarity and transforming American society into ‘a heterogeneous, incoherent, distracted mass.’A country’s dominion over its borders is a core aspect of national sovereignty. The abrogation of the 13 colonies’ authority to promote or restrict immigration as they deemed fit was among the principal grievances against the British crown listed in the Declaration of Independence.
