    #90081. 5 Books About Small Town Crime, from ‘Baby Queen’ Author Ty Landers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1076 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    5 Books About Small Town Crime, from ‘Baby Queen’ Author Ty Landers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1076 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Adjectives like streetwise and street-smart exist to acknowledge the specific intelligence needed to navigate the perils of urban living.
    • There’s plenty of menace in small places.
    • I write crime thrillers set in places where people only recently started locking their doors.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You expect danger in the city. Adjectives like streetwise and street-smart exist to acknowledge the specific intelligence needed to navigate the perils of urban living. Country intelligence has no succinct adjectives. Country-strong, that’s a thing. But, country-wise? More often than not, there is a misconception that life in the hinterlands will dull your edge, diminish your reflexes, lull you into a false sense of security.

    There’s plenty of menace in small places. In towns with no interstate ramp, nameless desert stops with no cell phone service, a desperate farm community surrounded by an ocean of corn.

    I write crime thrillers set in places where people only recently started locking their doors. These don’t have to be set in the South—mine are—but they can happen anywhere. Maybe it’s Southern noir when done south of the Mason-Dixon line. Rural noir is a good name, and throws its arms around the whole genre, but it’s a mouthful. It comes out sounding slurry, even when I’m sober, and might not come out at all if I’ve had a cocktail. This subgenre of crime fiction goes by many names. I wish I could just tell people I wrote Southerns and have them understand—the way most people understand the Western. Till then, here are five of my favorite examples of novels that take place out past the last lights of town.

    Recent findings suggest that important note: I had to leave out a lot of authors I adore and beg you to read anything and everything by the following for outstanding examples of small-town, insular, tight-nit, and Sun-Belt crime: Flannery O’Connor, S.A. Cosby, Carson McCullers, Henry Wise, Attica Locke, Dennis Lehane, Megan Abbott, Ivy Pochoda, and Elmore Leonard. Please find them.

    Daniel Woodrell is incredible. I love every word he has ever written but Tomato Red is my favorite. It opens with a gorgeous run-on sentence that’s almost three hundred words long and, after reading it, it’s almost impossible not to collapse and read the whole book in one sitting. The novel’s hapless anti-hero, Sammy Barlach—recently fired from a dog food factory and fresh off a speed-fueled burglary attempt—throws in with siblings Jason and Jamalee Merridew. Jason, a local object of female obsession, and his sister Jamalee want to weaponize Jason’s beauty, blackmail wealthy woman, and get them both out of Venus Holler. Sammy hitches his wagon to the Merridew’s scheme. But for Jason, a gay man in the hills and hollows of the Ozarks, choosing to live an authentic life proves to me more dangerous than one of crime.

    One of my favorite sayings from Tod Goldberg is that he writes about bad people doing terrible things to even worse people. In The Low Desert, he demonstrates this across twelve sometimes-connected stories set on the outskirts of California and Nevada. There are lonely deserts, fading resort towns, lost highways. Each story is a banger, but the fact that Goon Number Four isn’t your favorite TV show of the last decade is a miscarriage of justice. A story about a hired gun who enrolls in a community college, seeking to be rid of the life, only to find exploitation waiting in the halls of normalcy. The Low Desert has something I have never been able to fully articulate—feeling more like a great album, than the seminal work of crime fiction it is.

    Industry observers note that A personal favorite, Thompson’s Pop. 1280 is a novel that perfectly balances menace and comedy. Nick Corey, a terrible sheriff, oversees the 1280 souls of Potts County, Texas. Many of Nick’s constituents don’t want a sheriff, prefer to skirt the law, and tolerate him because he is pathologically shiftless. Our sheriff eats five meals a day, sleeps with any woman who’s up for it, sees murder as the only option rather than a last resort, and will do anything to keep his job. Not because he is ambitious, but because being sheriff allows him to do almost nothing. But, on the precipice of a difficult reelection, he reluctantly springs into action. Through the ensuing morass, Nick confronts sassy pimps, his pushy wife and her brother, his mistress and her husband, the town as whole, and the very concept of righteousness. Corey is a man who seems dumb, but isn’t. Someone dangerous and ruthless in the most peculiar and befuddling ways.

    Cormac McCarthy, No Country for Old Men.

    It has been revealed that cormac McCarthy’s most accessible novel. It is a literary crime novel that dissects the corrosive effects of money, heightened to break-neck entertainment by the inclusion of one of fiction’s most unforgettable bad dudes. In many ways, this is Anton Chigurh’s book the way Jaws belongs to the shark. Chigurh, a relentless hitman who’s as dangerous to his employers as he is to his targets, is evil with biblical scope. Ed-Tom Bell is a good man fading. A sheriff having and existential crisis, struggling to adapt to the requirements of his calling in a world where criminality has moved past opportunism and into something inconceivable. Throw in Llewelyn Moss, a Vietnam vet who stumbles across two million dollars after a drug deal goes wrong, and you’re in for a ride. When Chigurh’s tide of malevolence come in. One man tries to stem it, the other retreats. Fates are decided by the flip of a coin.

    Frank Bill, Crimes in Southern Indiana.

    Frank Bill’s debut, Crimes in Southern Indiana, is a cold look at a brutal version of Indiana that exists off the interstates. Southern Indiana is an anomaly—not quite the South, not quite the Midwest. Claimed by none—like the folks Bill writes about. He drops seventeen stories about this distinct region across two hundred and seventy pages in an achingly authentic voice. He can do more damage in ten pages than most other savvy word-geeks could with a lifetime supply of paper. The Penance of Scoot McCutchen will wreck you. I think about it all the time.

    According to recent reports, ty Landers holds an MFA in Creative Writing and Writing for the Performing Arts from the University of California, Riverside. Born and raised in Alabama, he spent more than twenty years in Nashville, Tennessee, before moving to Milwaukee, Wisconsin, with his wife and sons. His debut novel BABY QUEEN, out on November 17, 2026, is being adapted by HBO. For more on Ty Landers, visit: https://www.tylandersfiction.com/.

    • In a recent development, six months later in May 2026 Moldaliev was charged with inciting "mass unrest"—vague charges frequently brought against social media users in Kyrgyzstan who are prosecuted for sharing or resharing content online.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that A district court in Bishkek on November 11 sentenced Baktybek Moldaliev, an activist, to three years in jail for allegedly reposting content produced by Kloop Media, which a court had previously declared “extremist”. The case sends a chilling message to social media consumers across Kyrgyzstan: simply clicking the repost button on a social media platform could land someone in prison.

    Moldaliev, 49, who worked as a welder, and commented regularly on politics on Facebook was first detained for a day in November 2025, when police seized his phone as evidence and gained access to it, according to his wife, Elvira Zhusupova.

    In a recent development, six months later in May 2026 Moldaliev was charged with inciting "mass unrest"—vague charges frequently brought against social media users in Kyrgyzstan who are prosecuted for sharing or resharing content online. He was taken into custody where he has remained since. After a month and a half, authorities changed the charges to the production and distribution of extremist materials.

    During the November 11 court hearing, Moldaliev denied the allegations, saying that police or other individuals could have used his account to share the content and frame him.

    In a recent development, in July 2025, amid a crackdown on independent media, amendments to the criminal code and the code of offenses went into effect that toughen sanctions for production and distribution of materials authorities deem “extremist.” The crime is punishable by up to three years in prison, even without intent to disseminate the materials. The amendments also criminalize using the internet or mass media to make public calls for extremist activity, which carries a three to five-year prison sentence.

    In October 2025 a district court in Bishkek declared the activities of Rinat Tukhvashin, Kloop's co-founder, and investigative journalist Bolot Temirov, founder of Temirov LIVE and Ait-Ait Dese, as well as materials produced by their media outlets, “extremist”. It was the first time a court had declared the content of media outlets extremist, Kloop said.

    The Kyrgyz authorities should drop the case against Moldaliev, vacate his unjust conviction and release him, and the government should reverse course on its assault on the right to freedom of expression, stop weaponizing the criminal justice system to silence critics, and reform laws on extremism.

    #90077. Breaking: Chuck Thompson on the mysterious deaths of two Bigfoot hunters in Washington

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Chuck Thompson on the mysterious deaths of two Bigfoot hunters in Washington

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (988 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Skamania county rarely, if ever, captures the attention of the national news media.
    • On Christmas morning 2024, two men from Portland, Oregon, were reported missing in the wilds of Washington state.
    • “Two Portland men searching for Sasquatch and missing since early Christmas morning were found dead in the Gifford Pinchot National Forest—likely from exposure and being ill prepared,” the station reported.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Skamania county rarely, if ever, captures the attention of the national news media. Let alone the international news media. But during the traditionally slow Christmas holiday, when even serious outlets stoop to tracking Santa’s progress across the northern hemisphere and presenting expert commentary on decorations at the White House, the story about the bodies found in the backwoods of the Pacific Northwest arrived like a Christmas gift from News Kringle.

    On Christmas morning 2024, two men from Portland, Oregon, were reported missing in the wilds of Washington state. After a three-day search that involved more than sixty volunteers from two states, dogs, drones, and helicopters working through harsh terrain, icy conditions, and a snowstorm, their frozen bodies were recovered. On December 28, Portland’s CBS television affiliate KOIN 6 was among the first to pick up the story.

    “Two Portland men searching for Sasquatch and missing since early Christmas morning were found dead in the Gifford Pinchot National Forest—likely from exposure and being ill prepared,” the station reported.

    Did someone say Sasquatch? Every editor in the world knew clickbait when they saw it. Within days, near-identical headlines appeared around the world, backed by the biggest names in news.

    CNN: 2 Oregon men die from exposure in a forest after they went out to look for Sasquatch.

    Fox News: 2 dead after search for Sasquatch in Washington national forest.

    NPR: 2 men were found dead from exposure after looking for Sasquatch.

    BBC: Two men found dead while searching for Bigfoot.

    Nine News Australia: Two men found dead in US after going on Christmas Eve hunt for Bigfoot.

    Hundreds, perhaps thousands, jumped in. The Associated Press. MSN. CBS News. HuffPost. Newsweek. Today. Yahoo News. USA Today. Newly introduced York Post. Los Angeles Times. San Francisco Chronicle. The Times. Daily Mail.

    According to recent reports, the story was such a surefire traffic pusher that even specialized outlets ran with it. People. Sports Illustrated. AccuWeather. The celebrity and entertainment website TooFab. Spain’s national sports tabloid Marca. New Zealand’s Stuff. Taiwanese tabloid CTWant. The massively popular 52hrtt, a Chinese-language website that serves the global Chinese diaspora.

    There was no video, so each outlet looped the same images from a package of photos released by the Skamania County 23 sasquatch country Sheriff’s Office: four SAR volunteers on a snow-covered trail carrying an extension ladder through the forest; six volunteers in safety-orange jackets and helmets, one pointing a finger into the woods, using an extension ladder laid on the ground to cross a stream; a guy on hands and knees crawling across the ladder over a stream; a group of seven searchers using downed logs to cross a stream; and a Coast Guard helicopter hovering above an opening in the forest canopy.

    According to recent reports, in a digitally powered echo chamber, local, regional, national, and international outlets repeated the story almost word for word. All the way across the continent, News Center Maine television led its December 30 national news roundup in typical fashion:.

    In a recent development, we’ll start in Washington state. Two men were found dead there after going on a search for Bigfoot. They went out on their search a few days before Christmas Eve. When they didn’t return, family members contacted police. They were found after a three-day search. Local authorities there say it seems as though they likely died of exposure because of the weather conditions at the time and not being prepared.

    Sasquatch hunters. Christmas search. Poorly prepared. Died of exposure. That was all anyone seemed to know.

    Recent findings suggest that in fact, those elementary pieces of the story were all anyone in the news media actually did know. As even a cursory examination of the torrent of articles and broadcasts about the two bodies found in the forest showed, the stories were noteworthy mostly for their striking uniformity and lack of information. But something about the story wasn’t right. Something didn’t add up.

    Recent findings suggest that the rule that credible journalists are meant to follow is that the details in a story must support its headline—particularly if that headline makes an audacious claim. Two guys froze to death while looking for Bigfoot? Wow. Bring on the details.

    But that was the thing about the story of the Christmas Sasquatch hunters. After the stun-gun heds and ledes, there were no details about the supposed Sasquatch hunt. Not scant details. Not vague details. No details whatsoever. As if by mandate, every outlet that picked up the story made sure to include Sasquatch in its headline and opening grab. Then they dropped the Bigfoot angle altogether.

    Sources indicate that how long had the men been out looking for Sasquatch? Did they have a track record as Sasquatch hunters? Were they carrying special equipment, such as video cameras, long-range microphones, or telephoto lenses? If they were out searching for Sasquatch in rugged terrain and winter conditions, why were they so ill prepared?

    On these and other questions related to the Sasquatch hunt teased in the headlines, every story was the same—strangely mute.

    Excerpted from Sasquatch Country: Death, Myth, and Truth in the New American Wilderness by Chuck Thompson via Counterpoint Press.

    Industry observers note that chuck Thompson is the longtime editor of Columbia Insight, an award-winning environmental and outdoor news website based in Hood River, Oregon, just across the Columbia River from Skamania County and the Gifford Pinchot National Forest. A former executive producer with CNN.com, deputy editor of Men’s Journal, and Outside magazine contributor, he’s the author The Status Revolution: The Improbable Story of How the Lowbrow Became the Highbrow; the widely reviewed political screed Better Off Without ’Em: A Northern Manifesto for Southern Secession; the acclaimed travel memoir Smile When You’re Lying: Confessions of a Rogue Travel Writer; and Sasquatch Country: Death, Myth, and Truth in the New American Wilderness.

    • Nicolas Tiangaye, a prominent Central African lawyer, human rights defender, and former prime minister died in Bangui on November 16, at the age of 70.
    • Industry observers note that tiangaye first came into the spotlight as a young lawyer when he defended the former emperor, Jean-Bédel Bokassa, in 1986.
    • For Tiangaye, the cardinal rule that all defendants must benefit from their right to a fair trial is one he lived by.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Nicolas Tiangaye, a prominent Central African lawyer, human rights defender, and former prime minister died in Bangui on November 16, at the age of 70. One of the country's most respected rule of law advocates, his career spanned more than four decades.

    Industry observers note that tiangaye first came into the spotlight as a young lawyer when he defended the former emperor, Jean-Bédel Bokassa, in 1986. Later he defended the future president, François Bozizé, when he was accused of plotting a coup.

    For Tiangaye, the cardinal rule that all defendants must benefit from their right to a fair trial is one he lived by. By the early 1990s, Tiangaye was one of the leading Central African human rights advocates and served as the Bar Association president.

    In 1996 he was the lead defense council for Jean-Paul Akayesu before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. Human Rights Watch strongly advocated for the prosecution of Akayesu hailing his 1998 conviction as a historic international precedent. I once discussed the seminal conviction with Tiangaye and he reiterated that a good lawyer must be willing to defend clients and insist on due process, even in highly charged circumstances.

    Throughout the 1990s and 2000s, he spoke out for judicial independence and democratic governance. This often put him at odds with the government. But threats, he said, came with the job.

    In a recent development, he regularly ended up at the heart of national politics. Following Bozizé's successful coup, Tiangaye helped draft the 2004 Constitution. In January 2013, then-president Bozizé appointed Tiangaye prime minister amidst national turmoil. He remained in the position after Seleka seized Bangui and committed widespread abuses. Tiangaye despised the Seleka’s crimes, he told me, and he resigned.

    According to recent reports, he returned to legal practice and his passion: defending the Constitution. He became an outspoken critic of President Faustin-Archange Touadéra's efforts to remove presidential term limits, insisting on constitutional safeguards and political pluralism.

    It has been revealed that his death is both a professional and personal loss for Human Rights Watch. More importantly, it occurs as independent voices and institutions remain under pressure in the Central African Republic. I spoke with him just last week about detained activists. I wish I asked how he would like to be remembered. I imagine he would have insisted that we not focus on the individual, but on his commitment to the rule of law and human rights—Tiangaye’s ultimate legacy.

    #90075. Industry News: 5 gloriously unhinged speculative mysteries and thrillers

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1153 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: 5 gloriously unhinged speculative mysteries and thrillers

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1153 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, when a reviewer raved about my upcoming thriller, The Sleeper, with the words, “I love whatever is wrong with her,” I was delighted.
    • But this is not a modern phenomenon, there is a rich literary tradition of wild and crazy thrillers.
    • Robert Louis Stevenson, Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, when a reviewer raved about my upcoming thriller, The Sleeper, with the words, “I love whatever is wrong with her,” I was delighted. It’s my eighth book. With each one I’ve taken a bigger, bolder, and yes, a more unhinged swing. And I’m not alone. There is a rabid pack of unhinged thriller writers out there, and we’re only getting more bananas.

    But this is not a modern phenomenon, there is a rich literary tradition of wild and crazy thrillers. In fact, I’ve found it incredibly hard to whittle this list down to just five. This list bounces between the new, the nearly new and the really rather old.

    Robert Louis Stevenson, Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde.

    In a recent development, one of those novels so powerful that it becomes a conceptual byword (by-phrase?) used even by people who have never read it. Published in 1886 and so brisk it’s actually a novella, this unflinching gothic masterpiece still holds its own in 2026.

    There is almost as much mythology about the writing of the book as is contained in its pages. Stevenson claimed that it sprang from a wild nightmare that contained three scenes and the central idea, “of a voluntary change becoming involuntary.” His step-son claimed it was written in a three-day fit of pique. His wife claimed that Stephenson burned the first version after she suggested he was writing an allegory, which riled him up before he realized he agreed, and then started again.

    Industry observers note that stephenson’s health at the time was dire, he was on medication to stop his lungs hemorrhaging, which could have stimulated the originating nightmare. According to some rumors he was also taking cocaine, which could also explain the mad work rate and agitation….

    If you haven’t read it recently (or perhaps ever), you may raise an eyebrow at its inclusion in a list of thrillers but it more than earns its place.

    We have unreliable characters, memory blackouts, dual personalities and a race to stop a killer. And it’s actually, I would argue, a speculative thriller given that the whole problem starts with Dr Jekyll experimenting to create a serum that can overcome the dark parts of his personality. Instead, the serum splits him into two—the good Dr Jekyll, and the evil Mr Hyde.

    Sarah Pinborough, Behind Her Eyes.

    It has been revealed that I know this came out nearly ten years ago but I’m still agape at its twists. Sarah Pinborough tore up the rule book with this one, and proved that you could still find fresh ways to shock a savvy audience of thriller readers.

    If you’ve not read it, I don’t want to give anything away but what starts as a tense psychological thriller about a single mum having an affair with her boss while forming a close friendship with the boss’s wife, soon takes a hard swerve into lucid dreaming, astral projection and a past timeline exploring trauma and mental illness. And if that sounds heavy and gloomy, I’m doing it a massive disservice because it is an absolute rollercoaster.

    The ending was so WILD that it was a key part of the marketing, with the hashtag #WTFthatending spreading through Book Twitter (this was 2017, after all…).

    Lisa Jewell, None Of This Is True.

    It has been revealed that as a long-term fan, I loved watching the queen of women’s fiction become the doyenne of domestic suspense before winding her way down an ever-darker garden path. But Lisa Jewell’s 2023 novel, None Of This Is True, was a real escalation.

    A fever dream of lies, paranoia and platonic limerence. Alix is a successful true crime podcaster who meets her “birthday twin,” Josie, an unassuming local woman born on the same day but whose life is very different.

    They both have secrets, of course, which I’m loathe to give away but the novel is unflinching around dark topics like grooming, alcoholism and family dysfunction. For all its sucker punches (and the twists are *brain exploding emoji*) this is a nuanced and heartfelt exploration of the stories we tell ourselves in order to survive.

    In a recent development, if you were an unemployed gambling addict unable to pay your debts and whose loved ones were being threatened by the Yakuza, you’d take the first well-paid job that comes your way too, right? In this case, as a private chef to a reclusive billionaire in remote Japan.

    Soon, protagonist Ed is somewhat learning on the job in the best kitchen money can buy at the heart of an enormous mansion, with an endless supply of whatever ingredients the esoteric tastes of his boss desires….

    In a recent development, it’s been likened to Butter by Asako Yuzuki and there are overlaps in themes of greed, obsession and—of course—murder, but while Butter is a slow burn, Greedy is a runaway train. Messy, freaky and eye wateringly gory. I mean all those things as compliments!

    Fiona Cummins, Serial Killer Survivors Club.

    While 1980s teenager Robyn reels from the discovery that her father was a serial killer, her life is made infinitely worse by community ostracism and judgement.

    An experimental therapy group for the familial survivors of murderers changes her life, finally giving her the acceptance and friendship she has always craved. But when one of her new friends disappears in a town where three other young women are already missing, Robyn and her found-family risk everything to find them. After all, with their intimate knowledge of killers, the Serial Killer Survivors Club are the best hope these missing women have….

    I pat myself on the back for my ability to predict twists but this one spun me for a total loop. I was lucky enough to grab an advanced readers copy of this, which will be published next year in the UK and US. I highly recommend pre-ordering.

    My own unhinged thriller, The Sleeper, follows librarian Maya who falls asleep on a sleeper train and wakes up in a version of the world where history has changed overnight, her own life has been erased and nobody remembers her.

    Recent findings suggest that and the version of Britain she’s now living in? Just saying the wrong things can put you in the crosshairs of the state. Which is a massive problem for Maya, who in her bewilderment, has asked way too many questions already….

    Sources indicate that holly Seddon is the author of several thrillers, including the international bestseller Try Not to Breathe, The Hit List, and 59 Minutes. After growing up in the English countryside obsessed with music and books, Holly worked in London as a journalist and editor. After several years in Amsterdam, she now lives in Kent with her family and writes full time. Find out more at HollySeddon.com.

    #90074. The First Amendment, University Investigations, and Anti-Israel Lawprof's Case Against Univ. of Kentucky

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1746 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    The First Amendment, University Investigations, and Anti-Israel Lawprof's Case Against Univ. of Kentucky

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1746 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that some excerpts from the longish decision Friday by Judge Benjamin Beaton (E.D.
    • This opinion addresses the latest chapter in the ongoing saga concerning Professor Ramsi Woodcock, his commentary regarding Israel and Palestine, and the University of Kentucky's investigation into whether he violated Title VI or the school's technology or conduct policies….
    • Earlier this month, this Court denied law professor Ramsi Woodcock's request to halt the University of Kentucky's ongoing investigation into several comments he made related to his views on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and his 2025 "Petition for Military Action Against Israel." Woodcock's initial submissions had not persuasively shown that the investigation was retaliatory in its origin or chilling in its ongoing effect.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that some excerpts from the longish decision Friday by Judge Benjamin Beaton (E.D. Ky.) in Woodcock v. Capilouto:.

    This opinion addresses the latest chapter in the ongoing saga concerning Professor Ramsi Woodcock, his commentary regarding Israel and Palestine, and the University of Kentucky's investigation into whether he violated Title VI or the school's technology or conduct policies….

    Earlier this month, this Court denied law professor Ramsi Woodcock's request to halt the University of Kentucky's ongoing investigation into several comments he made related to his views on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and his 2025 "Petition for Military Action Against Israel." Woodcock's initial submissions had not persuasively shown that the investigation was retaliatory in its origin or chilling in its ongoing effect.

    But the order set an evidentiary hearing two weeks later to address these fact-dependent questions and Woodcock's request for a preliminary injunction. The investigation—which had lasted more than a year and whose report was already overdue—could not "last forever" without threatening Woodcock's First Amendment rights. And the University of Kentucky's corresponding "reassignment" of Woodcock from teaching duties throughout the investigation was increasingly hard to justify, particularly given the absence of any articulated suspicion of classroom disruption….

    Industry observers note that then, one week after the TRO decision, the outside investigator's 134-page sealed (for now) report finally landed. {That report is provisionally under seal pending the resolution of a motion to seal, which will be referred to a Magistrate Judge.} ….

    [Now], the Dean of the law school could decide whether to lift Woodcock's reassignment from teaching and restore him to the classroom for the spring semester. This could happen as late as mid-December, according to counsel, without prejudicing Woodcock's ability to teach…. [And] the University President could decide, based on the investigative report, whether (in his view) Woodcock violated any laws or policies….

    In a recent development, the report and Woodcock's response have been published by the Kentucky Lantern (McKenna Horsley); Woodcock reports that this is because they were publicly filed in a parallel state case. The court had this to say about Woodcock's request for a temporary injunction to block any findings by the University President:.

    During previous hearings, this Court observed that Woodcock's effort to end his reassignment from teaching stood on firmer ground that his request to halt the investigation itself. That view rested largely on caselaw that contemplated speech-related investigations consistent with the First Amendment yet considered whether any attendant consequences of such investigations abridged those rights based on a retaliatory purpose, chilled speech, or both. {See generally, e.g., Sensabaugh v. Halliburton (6th Cir. 2019) (no adverse action based on "letter of guidance" and reprimand in the context of a "independent law firm" investigation involving "scores of documents and text messages" and "seventeen different witnesses"); Moore v. Garnand (9th Cir. 2023) ("[W]e never held that a retaliatory investigation alone could violate the First Amendment, as our holding rested on much more than just a retaliatory investigation[.]").} ….

    Woodcock insists that the First Amendment bars the President from spending "weeks poring over documents" unrelated to "any arguable policy violation." "Whatever the University decides about spring teaching, findings issued on the investigator's report would injure Woodcock irreparably on their own." To the extent that review entails an inquiry into his political beliefs, Woodcock contends, the process is illegitimate and should be enjoined immediately….

    It has been revealed that [But] a substantial body of caselaw indicates that a speech-related investigation alone generally doesn't amount to retaliation or adverse action. {See, e.g., Churchill v. Univ. of Colorado at Boulder (Colo. App. 2010) ("Courts have concluded that investigations alone are not adverse employment actions."); Sensabaugh (6th Cir. 2019) (concluding no adverse action even when context included a "painstakin[g] investigation"); Couch v. Board. of Trustees of Memorial Hospital of Carbon County (10th Cir. 2009) (investigation didn't amount to adverse action supporting First Amendment retaliation); Benningfield v. City of Houston (5th Cir. 1998) ("Although a reprimand can constitute an adverse employment action, an investigation does not[.]"); Moore ("[W]e have never held that a retaliatory investigation alone could violate the First Amendment"); Bell v. Sheriff of Broward County 1375 (11th Cir. 2021) ("[D]eputy Bell's five-day suspension with pay pending an investigation into his conduct is not an adverse action."). But as emphasized in the Court's previous TRO opinion, the caselaw in this area is hardly uniform and uncertainty remains about how different circuits might approach each specific factual scenario. See, e.g., Holt v. Pennsylvania (3d Cir. 2017) ("Our Circuit has not considered whether the initiation of an internal investigation can constitute an 'adverse action' for purposes of a First Amendment retaliation claim, and our sister circuits are split on the glitch.").} The collateral consequences of an investigation, by contrast, may create an intolerable chill that could warrant judicial intervention. See, e.g., Levin v. Harleston (2d Cir. 1992); White v. Lee (9th Cir. 2000). The First Amendment leaves at least some room for employers to investigate their employees for perceived misconduct, even when the alleged offenses relate to speech. Waters v. Churchill (1994) (plurality op.) ("Only [investigative] procedures outside the range" of reasonableness violate First Amendment despite investigation's "risk of erroneously punishing protected speech."); Gartenberg v. Cooper Union (S.D.N.Y. 2025) (even protected speech may be relevant to determining "whether actionable harassment occurred").

    In a recent development, woodcock hasn't pointed to any precedent halting a school's investigation based only on its existence or the "brand" or "reputational harm" that it might produce. To the contrary, the two precedents on which he relies most heavily are easily distinguishable.

    Sweezy v. Newly introduced Hampshire (1957), is a 70-year-old precedent concerning a state attorney general's investigation into a professor's affiliation with the Communist and Progressive Parties. It had little, if anything, to say about the operations, autonomy, or academic interests of a university. Contra, e.g., Regents of University of Michigan v. Ewing (1985).

    Fischer v. Thomas (6th Cir. 2022), likewise sits far afield from the context of university governance and academic speech. In that pre-enforcement challenge, the Sixth Circuit barred a state judicial commission from initiating formal proceedings against two judicial candidates after it "sen[t] vague and threatening letter to [the] candidates on the eve of election." The opinion didn't address whether an investigation or its concluding findings amounted to adverse action or retaliation….

    Fifth, even assuming Woodcock could establish a likelihood of success on the merits of his retaliation claim, to obtain a TRO he'd have to show irreparable harm and the balance of the equities relative to third parties and the public. Irreparable harm likely requires at least some showing of subjective chill as well; otherwise a court would be left to wonder why and "whether it needs to act now." ….

    The current record does precious little to "identify speech that [Woodcock] wishes to make in the future but for the threat of prosecution of that future speech." Despite boilerplate assertions that he'd otherwise say and write more about Israel and Palestine, it's hardly clear that this investigation has chilled Woodcock's speech at all. He points to a paper called "A Law and Economics Argument for Ending Israel" that he hasn't yet submitted to the law reviews; diminished posting on his blog, called "the Antizionist Legal Studies Movement;" and allegedly decreased Twitter activity. Yet Woodcock's social-media and listserv posting hasn't stopped altogether; during this investigation he has continued to post on X and the AALS online discussion groups, including about Israel; he has filed at least four lawsuits, several of which have been covered in the press; he maintains a webpage supplying information about and soliciting support for his speech and litigation. Without further evidence, the Court cannot conclude that Woodcock will be chilled over the next two weeks.

    Although the general tendency in the caselaw to treat First Amendment violations as irreparable harm cautions against assigning dispositive weight to this factor, the weakness of Woodcock's showing on the current record at least cuts against automatic or presumptive injunctive relief to ameliorate any purported self-censorship….

    The court also pointed to the university's own interest in speaking about Woodcock's speech:.

    Sources indicate that [A]n injunction barring the President from reacting to the investigator's findings would—even on Woodcock's own terms—remedy one arguable free-speech violation with another. As any law professor knows, Justice Brandeis taught that the "remedy" for disfavored speech should ordinarily be more speech—not additional suppression. A college president, just like a law professor, may presumptively speak—privately or publicly—about a matter of public and professional interest such as this. Indeed, both have done so during this process.

    According to recent reports, and President Capiluto's own speech rights aren't the only countervailing interests at glitch. The University has its own governance interests in the orderly and prompt resolution of a high-profile pending investigation. See Ewing ("Academic freedom thrives not only on the independent and uninhibited exchange of ideas among teachers and students, … but also, and somewhat inconsistently, on autonomous decisionmaking by the academy itself."). "Without this ability to investigate, a public employer would be left without recourse and would lose its 'greater leeway in its dealings with citizen employees.'".

    Given these compounding considerations, the Court concluded that no temporary order revisiting the Court's prior orders and specifically restraining the President was warranted based on these allegations of objective chill (regarding Woodcock's likelihood of success on the merits), subjective chill (regarding any irreparable harm associated with Woodcock's speech pending the forthcoming presidential findings), or the public and third-party interest in an orderly and prompt conclusion to an academic investigation….

    This order, to be clear, does not resolve whether the University officials' past actions constituted retaliation in violation of the First Amendment—a distinct and retrospective question, for which damages and attorney fees under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1983 & 1988 are at least potentially available (though the Defendants of course disagree). While those historical facts are necessary to Woodcock's showing of likelihood of success on the merits, even if proved they are not sufficient to warrant a restraining order, which requires a showing of ongoing chilled speech.

    Industry observers note that nor does this order address the propriety of any discipline that Woodcock might eventually face. As described above, those questions haven't ripened and follow their own administrative process—one the Sixth Circuit specifically contemplated might alter the abstention analysis….

    It has been revealed that as world leaders recently gathered in Phnom Penh to celebrate the 20th Francophonie Summit with the theme of peace and shared prosperity, French President Emmanuel Macron took to the podium to call publicly for an investigation into the killing of former Cambodian lawmaker and French citizen Lim Kimya. It was a rare public rebuke of the Cambodian government by a foreign leader.

    According to recent reports, A gunman killed Kimya in Bangkok, Thailand in January 2025. Kimya had served as a parliament member with the opposition Cambodia National Rescue Party before its 2017 dissolution.

    A Thai court convicted the gunman, Ekkalak Paenoi, in October 2025 and issued arrest warrants for two Cambodian suspects, Ly Ratanakraksmey and Pich Kimsrin, both of whom have connections to high-ranking Cambodian officials. The Cambodian government—like many of its neighbors in Southeast Asia—is increasingly persecuting activists abroad.

    The Cambodian government has yet to acknowledge the arrest warrants or start an impartial investigation. Both men remain at large. France has issued Interpol Red Notices for them on charges of complicity in premeditated murder.

    It has been revealed that macron’s raising Kimya’s murder during a joint press conference with Prime Minister Hun Manet sends a strong message that the French government is taking Cambodian authorities’ attacks on activists abroad seriously. The Cambodian government should heed the call and independently and impartially investigate the murder.

    In a recent development, but political repression by the Cambodian government runs deeper than one case. Ahead of 2027 local elections, the authorities are escalating their crackdown on the long suppressed political opposition. Young activists in particular, such as the five imprisoned Mother Nature Cambodia environmental activists, have been punished with baseless treason charges and lengthy prison sentences. Concerned governments should publicly and privately urge Cambodian authorities to release the more than 100 Cambodians right now imprisoned for exercising their fundamental freedoms.

    According to recent reports, human Rights Watch was among the local and international organizations that pressed Cambodian authorities to release the Mother Nature activists and others ahead of the Francophonie Summit. The ruling Cambodian People’s Party, which exerts complete control over the country’s courts, was apparently unbothered by these efforts.

    Other foreign leaders should amplify Macron’s message and publicly call on Cambodia’s government to reopen the space for the political opposition and respect the fundamental rights of all Cambodians, both at home and abroad.

    #90071. Sacha Naspini on the human stories behind Italy’s tomb-raider subculture.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2223 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Sacha Naspini on the human stories behind Italy’s tomb-raider subculture.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2223 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Bardo Sacchetti has the people of the Val di Cornia wrapped around his little finger.
    • Sources indicate that when Bardo suddenly disappears, his son, Veleno, takes over the family business and old relationships between the gang and the milieu in which it operates begin to fray.
    • In a recent development, sacha Naspini’s compact and suspenseful upcoming novel, The Witch’s Mouth (2026, Europa, translated by Clarissa Botsford), drops you in the midst of the action, and creates a world peopled with crooks and cooks, a prostitute, heir-apparent, fishmonger, marquis.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Tuscany, 1972. Bardo Sacchetti has the people of the Val di Cornia wrapped around his little finger. Thanks to him and his band of tomb raiders, locals in the impoverished region can now buy fridges for their homes or give their kids an education. He asks for nothing in return except for gratitude.

    Sources indicate that when Bardo suddenly disappears, his son, Veleno, takes over the family business and old relationships between the gang and the milieu in which it operates begin to fray. Former alliances fall apart and Bardo’s empire looks like it might be destroyed by violence. Veleno has some massive decisions to make.

    In a recent development, sacha Naspini’s compact and suspenseful upcoming novel, The Witch’s Mouth (2026, Europa, translated by Clarissa Botsford), drops you in the midst of the action, and creates a world peopled with crooks and cooks, a prostitute, heir-apparent, fishmonger, marquis. The story unfolds from their perspectives.

    I sent written questions to Naspini, and Edoardo Andreoni translated his written responses from Italian into English. The interview has been edited for length.

    Radha Vatsal: Let’s start with some background. Tuscany, where the novel takes place, seems to be littered with antiquities. Is this more the case in Tuscany than in other parts of Italy? Can you describe some of the types of antiquities that have been found there in recent years?

    Sources indicate that sacha Naspini: Actually, that’s true of pretty much all of Italy. It’s a country where history has accumulated over millennia, layer upon layer. Here, even a routine excavation can turn into an archaeological discovery.

    It has been revealed that tuscany is no exception. In fact, it’s one of the regions where this historical layering is particularly evident, largely thanks to the Etruscan civilization, which preceded Roman rule. Discoveries are still being made today. Take the recent finds at San Casciano dei Bagni, near Siena: extraordinary bronzes, along with coins, crowns, jewelry, votive arms and heads….

    As for The Witch’s Mouth, the novel is set in a specific part of Tuscany, the Val di Cornia. It’s an area I know well, one that plays an vital role in the fictional universe of some of my novels. This was once home to Populonia, one of the most important Etruscan cities and the only one built directly on the coast. In the Gulf of Baratti, you can visit Etruscan necropolises, monumental tombs, burial chambers carved into the rock, and the remains of Etruscan and Roman settlements.

    According to recent reports, RV: The events in the novel occur in the early 1970s. Was there a particular reason for choosing this time period?

    SN: Yes, there is. Choosing this period was an exciting challenge, and one that felt necessary. The Witch’s Mouth was born out of long conversations with tomb raiders and smugglers who were active during that time. Suddenly I came across some truly extraordinary, almost unbelievable stories. That’s when I began thinking about using this material as the basis for a novel.

    Industry observers note that there were also three aspects that I found particularly fascinating. First of all, the “fever” I always noticed in the people who told me about their adventures. That’s the expression they would use: “digging fever.” It went beyond money or swashbuckling adventure—a special light would sparkle in their eyes. As these small-town Indiana Jones recalled those times, that almost addictive excitement was rekindled— the excitement of the moment when, after devising a proposal, they would finally manage to break into a burial site, the first people to set foot there in millennia. And then reach out and touch the objects… Part of my job was to try to capture their passion.

    The second aspect was even more intriguing and had to do specifically with the Val di Cornia. The trafficking of archaeological artifacts was already underway in other parts of Italy—for instance in the Tuscia region—but in this small corner of Tuscany, people were late to the game.

    I heard crazy stories of farmers whose cellars were filled with bronzes that had turned up when they were plowing the land, and who would give them to their grandchildren to play with, like toy soldiers. After storms at sea, amphorae would wash up on the shore at Baratti. Kids would place them on top of low walls and throw rocks at them. Women would show up at Mass on Sunday wearing earrings and necklaces found in the fields….

    So I wondered, what would happen if an entire community, largely made up of people who struggle to make ends meet, suddenly realized that their homes were full of objects they considered worthless but that could fetch millions on the black market?

    Sources indicate that as I was researching the historical archives of the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera, I came across a news story from 1971 about a twelve-inch bronze artifact seized by the Carabinieri. It was about to be sold to an American collector for half a billion lire (roughly $5 million in today’s money). People in that region had piles of similar bronzes, tossed aside in a corner.

    In a recent development, finally, a purely personal aspect. I spent part of my childhood and adolescence in that region. Other kids and I would form our own little gangs and sneak out of the house in the middle of the night armed, with ropes, shovels, and spades, and head off into the woods. We imagined we were living in The Goonies, but instead of searching for One-Eyed Willy’s treasure, we were searching for Etruscan artifacts. Thinking back on it, what mattered wasn’t so much finding something as the adventure itself. Entering the woods at night was a significant challenge. And then the thrill of digging, without really knowing where to look… In a way, I think I experienced some of that same fever the “professional” tomb raiders talked about.

    RV: The Witch’s Mouth is an ensemble novel with a lot of different characters, but it revolves around Bardo. He’s almost a godfather-type figure in the way he involves so many different kinds of people in his activities and spreads the wealth he earns. Tell us about your inspiration for creating him.

    SN: Everything that happens in the novel is inspired by the interviews I mentioned earlier. But the characters are entirely the product of my imagination, as are the main plot and the various subplots.

    Recent findings suggest that when it comes to Bardo, I did a little “plundering” myself. Based on the stories I heard, I imagined this guy who, even as a kid, recognized the value of these artifacts, which everyone else treated like useless old junk taking up space.

    Sources indicate that but Bardo is also a man of action, and a pretty clever one. He knows how hard life is for the families of Populonia. He starts getting them to hand over their “pieces,” as they call them in the trade, and then sells them to the more experienced tomb raiders in the Tuscia region, returning with the money. Real money, not a few pennies.

    Before long, everyone starts looking at Bardo like a sort of saint. Everyone is knocking on his door with an artifact in their hand. And Bardo is extremely good at weaving a network built on trust and gratitude. That means protection—Bardo is untouchable. This is something else that fascinated me: at least in the beginning, there wasn’t a gun in sight. But then the operation grows exponentially. Billions of lire start pouring in. And where there’s that much money, guns usually follow.

    RV: Of the novel’s many great characters, I was fascinated by Elisa, Bardo’s wife; Silvana, the prostitute; and the Marquis. As you write, do you have favorites? Do some of the characters come more easily to you than others?

    It has been revealed that SN: Obviously I love them all, not only because of the role they each play in the story—a character is always an opportunity to explore different points of view, different lives and legacies… What I mean is, how does a particular character, with their own history, react to certain events? That’s part of the magic of writing. Especially when we explore uncomfortable aspects of human nature and relationships.

    In a recent development, that noted, among the characters you mentioned, Silvana and the Marchese have a special place in my heart. Silvana truly is the queen (I should say, the Principessa) of the novel. The Marchese, for his part, embodies a desperation that is part of the landscape and is compounded by his broken dreams, a desperation that still moves me. Although in the end… but I’d better stop here.

    RV: In many ways, this is the story of a gang of tomb robbers but it’s also the story of an ecosystem of stolen goods and people.

    Sources indicate that SN: I had some interesting experiences in this respect during the promotion of the book in Italy. Together with my Italian publishers, we had the wonderful idea of organizing some events in archaeological museums. Some of the events were fantastic. In other cases, though, for instance in Vetulonia, the director of the magnificent local museum declined to participate. He didn’t want to celebrate, right in a place designed to house Etruscan artifacts, a story about thieves who had deprived everyone of the opportunity to admire works of art and experience the sense of connection we can feel with the people who lived in distant times.

    Recent findings suggest that but I’m not an educator; I’m a novelist. I try to make sense of the world through stories. Even if these stories are unsettling—in fact, all the better. What I’m saying is, “Hey, look, this happened too.” I’m saying, “Hey, look at how these people lived. How they reacted, what they dreamt about, what circumstances led them to make certain choices.” And I know very well that it’s wrong to prevent the public from viewing a work of art, locking it away instead in some billionaire’s safe.

    I’ll go further. For me, the real damage inflicted by tomb raiders is not the sale of a particular artifact to a private collector. The real theft—and maybe it’s the novelist in me talking—has to do with removing a clue (the artifact itself) from the place where it was found, thereby interrupting a story. Otherwise, archaeologists would be able to tell us how people loved, what clothes they wore or what food they ate, what gods they worshipped, what stories they passed down in that very place. This is what they rob us of, to make a few million dollars. I hope that somehow, between the lines of my novel, this message comes across. But according to some museum directors, I’ve missed the mark.

    RV: Are there other novels or writers you draw inspiration from in your work?

    In a recent development, SN: The list would be endless, stretching from my formative years to the present, now that I’ve just turned fifty. It would comprise all the different kinds of writing I’ve sought out, explored, and measured myself against. And yet I feel like I’m just starting out.

    To mention some writers that have a place in my heart, in no particular order: Italo Calvino, Stephen King, Albert Camus, Joyce Carol Oates, John Steinbeck, Chuck Palahniuk, Beppe Fenoglio, Ágota Kristóf, Mikhail Bulgakov. If you asked me again a minute from now, the list would be completely different. I’m thinking of John Fante, or the fantasy novels I adored as a teenager. And what about Dumas and his Count of Monte Cristo?

    Industry observers note that seriously, I never know how to answer this question. But I think that each of these writers has given me a great gift: they “gave me permission” to be brave. To let my imagination spill onto the page, for what it’s worth. And all the voices that come with it.

    RV: What are you reading and/or working on at the moment?

    Industry observers note that SN: On my nightstand are books by David Szalay and Ernest Jünger—the latter a special gift I received, a book that I’ve already read but want to reread. Recently, I returned to John Fante’s Wait Until Spring, Bandini after many years—what a knockout. I don’t think it will ever get old. I also really loved Tiffany McDaniel’s The Summer That Melted Everything.

    It has been revealed that on my computer is a novel forthcoming in Italy, Il ronzio (“The Buzzing”), which is in the final stages of editing. Of course, I’m also working on another novel. And I’m having fun writing the treatment for a TV series, which is due soon. And listen to this: after twenty years of writing books, for the first time ever, there’s a police inspector in one of my stories. I never would have imagined it.

    Radha Vatsal is the Film/TV Columnist for CrimeReads. She is the author of No. 10 Doyers Street and the Kitty Weeks mysteries, and her essays have appeared in the The Latest York Times, The Atlantic, the Los Angeles Review of Books, and elsewhere. She holds a Ph.D. in Film History from Duke University. You can find her on Instagram or email: rvatsal@lithub.com.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Journalists, activists and political opponents who fled Burkina Faso to escape the junta’s repression now risk arrest and prosecution abroad, as the country’s judicial authorities pursue dozens of individuals over alleged terrorism-related offenses.

    Burkina Faso Prosecutor General Désiré Sawadogo declared on November 13 that a special court handling terrorism-related offenses had opened six cases against at least 45 people and entities. All those targeted exposed serious military abuses during counterinsurgency operations and include exiled journalists critical of the junta, among them Ahmed Newton Barry, Issaka Lingani, Inoussa Ouédraogo, Adama Ouedraogo, and Abdoulaye Barry; exiled social media activist Naïm Touré; former foreign affairs minister Alpha Barry, and international journalist Wassim Nasr. They face various charges, including complicity in terrorist associations and financing terrorism.

    Burkina Faso sent international arrest warrants and extradition requests to Côte d’Ivoire, France, and the United States, remarked Sawadogo. He added that Burkina Faso asked the United States to use Meta to identify and prosecute Facebook page administrators accused of promoting terrorism.

    Sources indicate that the authorities are using counterterrorism laws to target critical voices and restrict independent reporting on military abuses. The extradition requests extend political repression beyond Burkina Faso’s borders, placing critics who sought protection abroad at risk of arrest, forced return, and further abuse. The government’s recent decision to reinstate capital punishment for offenses including terrorism, high treason, and espionage is also of grave concern.

    Since seizing power in a September 2022 coup, the junta has restricted fundamental rights through media bans, suspension of unions and civil society organizations, dissolution of political parties, enforced disappearances, and the unlawful conscription of government critics.

    Meanwhile, the conflict between government forces and allied militias and Islamist armed groups, ongoing since 2017, has involved widespread abuses by all parties, including war crimes and crimes against humanity, with no accountability. Human Rights Watch has documented serious flaws in the special terrorism court, including prolonged pretrial detention, and violations of fair trial guarantees.

    Concerned governments should rigorously scrutinize all extradition and judicial cooperation requests from Burkina Faso. No journalist, activist or political opponent should be returned where there are substantial grounds to fear torture, arbitrary detention, an unfair trial, and the death penalty. International partners should condemn the targeting of critics at home and abroad and reject Burkina Faso’s attempts at transnational repression.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (New York) – Nabeel Rajab, a prominent human rights activist from Bahrain and a close partner of Human Rights Watch, passed away on November 17, 2026, at the age of 62. He reportedly died in Türkiye following a heart attack.

    Sources indicate that rajab rose to prominence as a human rights defender in Bahrain in the 1990s, and in 2000 he co-founded the Bahrain Human Rights Society, one of Bahrain’s first human rights organizations. He then co-founded the Bahrain Centre for Human Rights in 2002, later becoming its president, and co-founded and was executive director of the Gulf Centre for Human Rights starting in 2011.

    Rajab had served as a member of the Human Rights Watch Middle East and North Africa division’s advisory committee since 2010, playing a key role not only in supporting Human Rights Watch work in Bahrain, but also providing guidance to the documentation and advocacy work that Human Rights Watch carries out across the region.

    Recent findings suggest that bahraini authorities unjustly detained and imprisoned him several times for his peaceful expression in the years following the 2011 pro-democracy protests in Bahrain. In 2018, he was sentenced to five years in prison for his comments criticizing torture at a Bahraini prison and the Saudi-led military campaign in Yemen. Even from detention, he continued his activism. In 2017, he wrote an op-ed for the Newly introduced York Times from detention, titled “Don’t Profit from Abuses by Bahrain,” calling out US support of Bahraini authorities despite their abuses both in Bahrain and amid the conflict in Yemen. He wrote:.

    Recent findings suggest that all our destinies are tied together. What will happen to Bahrain if everyone who supports peace, democracy and the rule of law is in jail? To whom will Bahrain’s disenfranchised youth turn to for support and guidance? These are the questions the Trump administration must ask itself before it sends my jailers another batch of fighter jets.

    It has been revealed that he was released from prison in 2020 and allowed to serve the rest of his sentence at home with his family, but only after his health deteriorated due to harsh detention conditions. In the years that followed, he continued to support the human rights movement and call out human rights abuses by Bahraini and other authorities across the world.

    According to recent reports, sayed Ahmed al-Wadaei, the advocacy director at the Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy and a close friend, said that Rajab left Bahrain in March 2026 so that he could speak publicly on Bahraini human rights complications. He remained in exile until his passing, unable to return to Bahrain for fear of being rearrested.

    Recent findings suggest that rajab’s death is a profound blow to the global and Arab human rights movements, which have lost a steadfast defender of freedom of expression and a voice of reason in a climate increasingly marked by hatred and polarization. Over many years, Rajab stood resolutely by his principles, despite being targeted, detained, and repressed for his unwavering commitment to universal human rights.

    “Nabeel was a stalwart champion for human rights and democracy, not just for Bahrain but all of the Middle East,” said Sarah Leah Whitson, former Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “He paid a tremendous price for his advocacy, jailed and abused in prison, but always kept us hopeful and resilient. He played an essential role in guiding and supporting the work of Human Rights Watch’s MENA division. I considered him a true friend.”.

    In a recent development, “Nabeel’s legacy lives on in the innumerable people he inspired, fought alongside in the defense of rights, and held up, sometimes in their darkest moments,” said Balkees Jarrah, Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “He has been a leader and guide to human rights defenders in the region. He and his family paid a high price for his activism, but we are grateful for his wisdom, tenacity, and courage.”.

    Nabeel Rajab’s courage, integrity, and principled advocacy will be his enduring legacy. Our thoughts are with his family, loved ones, and the many friends who mourn his loss.

    Sudan: Transfer War Crimes Suspects to ICC

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1034 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (The Hague) – Sudanese authorities should immediately transfer former Interior Minister Ahmed Haroun to the International Criminal Court (ICC) to face charges in The Hague, Human Rights Watch said today.
    • According to recent reports, on November 8, 2026, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) reportedly re-arrested Haroun, interior minister of Sudan in 2007, when an ICC arrest warrant was issued against him.
    • According to recent reports, “For two decades, victims of atrocity crimes in Darfur have witnessed Haroun and others evading justice, leading to impunity-fueled cycles of violence that are claiming more victims every day.” noted Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (The Hague) – Sudanese authorities should immediately transfer former Interior Minister Ahmed Haroun to the International Criminal Court (ICC) to face charges in The Hague, Human Rights Watch said today. Haroun was recently taken into Sudanese custody and faces ICC war crimes and crimes against humanity charges, committed in Sudan’s Darfur region, in 2003 and 2004.

    According to recent reports, on November 8, 2026, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) reportedly re-arrested Haroun, interior minister of Sudan in 2007, when an ICC arrest warrant was issued against him. He was arrested one day after he took part in a video podcast interview, his first public appearance since 2019. The armed forces have not officially confirmed Haroun’s whereabouts, but media reported that he is detained in Khartoum state.

    According to recent reports, “For two decades, victims of atrocity crimes in Darfur have witnessed Haroun and others evading justice, leading to impunity-fueled cycles of violence that are claiming more victims every day.” noted Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch. “If Sudan’s authorities transferred those sought by the ICC to the court in The Hague, as they are obliged to do, it would send a powerful message to those committing crimes today that they too may find themselves in the dock.”.

    Sources indicate that authorities should also transfer former President Omar al-Bashir—who is believed to be in Sudanese custody in Khartoum state as well—and locate, arrest, and transfer former Defense Minister Abdelrahim M. Hussein. The ICC has also issued arrest warrants for both of them, though there is no information available on Hussein’s location.

    In a recent development, the ICC issued an arrest warrant against Haroun in 2007, and another against Hussein in 2012, for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Darfur between 2003 and 2004. During that period, Sudanese government forces and allied militias carried out targeted attacks against civilians on the basis of their ethnicity, including killings, rape, forced displacement from their homes and land, and burning of their villages. In 2009 and 2010, the ICC issued two arrest warrants against al-Bashir for alleged war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide committed in Darfur between 2003 and 2008.

    Following al-Bashir’s ouster in April 2019, Sudanese authorities held Haroun, al-Bashir, and Hussein in custody for charges not related to atrocities in Darfur but failed to transfer them to the ICC.

    After fighting erupted between SAF and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on April 15, 2023, the authorities moved al-Bashir to Alia military hospital in Omdurman, Khartoum state, where he reportedly remained under guard, while Haroun left detention amid the collapse of prison security, and under circumstances suggesting coordination with judicial authorities.

    On September 30, 2026, SAF granted al-Bashir initial approval to travel outside of Sudan for medical treatment. Based on media reports, al-Bashir continues to receive medical care at Alia military hospital and is yet to travel abroad.

    According to recent reports, UN Security Council Resolution 1593, referring the situation in Darfur to the ICC prosecutor, requires the government of Sudan to cooperate with the court even though it is not a party to the Rome Statute, the ICC’s founding treaty. In 2021, the ICC’s Office of the Prosecutor signed a memorandum of understanding with the Sudanese authorities addressing cooperation for arrests. The ICC lacks the ability to enforce its own orders and relies on state cooperation to conduct investigations and make arrests.

    Recent findings suggest that in January and July, the Office of the Prosecutor reported to the United Nations Security Council on its investigation in Darfur, including its continued engagement with Sudanese authorities. In addition to addressing crimes from July 2002 onward, the Office of the Prosecutor is also investigating crimes committed since April 2023 in Darfur. The prosecutor’s office reported “positive” and “significant” cooperation by Sudanese authorities, and assistance in support of its investigative activities, including deployment of the office’s investigative team to Port Sudan.

    Nevertheless, Sudan has not fulfilled its obligation to carry out the court’s arrest warrants and transfer the wanted suspects to the Hague. The authorities should provide public information on the whereabouts of all the wanted suspects and take immediate steps to allow their transfer to the court, Human Rights Watch stated.

    The African Union, the members of the Atrocity Prevention and Justice Coalition for Sudan–– particularly the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and Sierra Leone––as well as the European Union and its member states should directly engage with Sudanese authorities, calling on them to comply with their obligation to fully cooperate with the ICC and to transfer Haroun, al-Bashir, and Hussein to the court’s custody.

    Recent findings suggest that ICC judges have referred to the Security Council several findings of noncooperation against Sudan and ICC member states in relation to the arrest of ICC suspects. However, the council has never taken steps to enforce these findings. UN member states should urge the Security Council to back the ICC’s mandate in Darfur, including by enforcing the court’s findings of noncooperation on arrests.

    The ICC prosecutor’s office should use its next biannual report to the council, in January 2027, as an opportunity to raise any concerns related to Sudan’s cooperation on arrests.

    In 2025, the ICC convicted Ali Muhammad Ali Abd-Al-Rahman (also known as Ali Kosheib), a former leader of Sudan’s “Janjaweed” militias, for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Darfur in 2003 and 2004, and sentenced him to 20 years in prison. Kosheib’s trial was possible after he surrendered himself voluntarily to the ICC’s custody in 2020.

    “For victims and survivors of crimes in Darfur, Sudanese authorities’ promises of cooperation mean little without concrete action,” Evenson said. “Sudan’s international partners should use every diplomatic tool at their disposal to press for the immediate transfer of all ICC suspects in Sudanese custody and make clear that cooperation with the court is not optional.”.
