    #90046. The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1728 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1728 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • One of the Supreme Court’s most critical functions is deciding what cases to decide.
    • This process has been explained before, but – given the court is now choosing what cases to hear next term – I’d like to use this column to examine some questions about the certiorari or “cert.” process, as it is known.
    • The vast majority of cases come to the Supreme Court in the form of petitions for certiorari, a Latin term meaning “to be more fully informed.” The court receives nearly 4,000 petitions each term and grants review to about 60.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    One of the Supreme Court’s most critical functions is deciding what cases to decide.

    This process has been explained before, but – given the court is now choosing what cases to hear next term – I’d like to use this column to examine some questions about the certiorari or “cert.” process, as it is known. As we shall see, some of these questions have answers; others do not.

    First, a review of the basics. The vast majority of cases come to the Supreme Court in the form of petitions for certiorari, a Latin term meaning “to be more fully informed.” The court receives nearly 4,000 petitions each term and grants review to about 60. By a 100-year-old tradition, review is granted when four of the nine justices want to hear a case. When this occurs, the parties file briefs and the justices hear oral argument before issuing their decision.

    This process is a blend of transparent argument and secretive deliberation. The transparent portion is that the losing party in a lower court, the petitioner, files a public petition for certiorari, making the best case for why the court should resolve the legal issue in the case. The winner in the lower court, the respondent, also spells out why the court does not need to review the ruling of the lower court. After that, however, the case disappears into the halls and procedures of the high court.

    Question one: how does the court handle and process the petitions?

    According to recent reports, as noted, by 100-year-old custom, it takes four votes for the court to agree to review a case (the “rule of four”). But the vote to grant or deny cert. is not public. We do not know if a petition met with overwhelming consensus that review was necessary or not, or whether it scraped by or just missed out on being granted.

    Nor do we know why the court declines to review a case. When the court agrees to decide a case, the final opinion is likely to make clear why the justices were interested. Denials of cert. petitions, however, are not accompanied by any explanation, except in the few instances when an individual justice writes a dissent from the denial of a petition. Justice Sonia Sotomayor, for example, sometimes points out in a dissent or concurrence what she deems to be an crucial problem of individual rights in criminal cases. But such dissents are relatively infrequent.

    This can be frustrating to counsel: Just how much interest an unsuccessful petition attracted would be useful to lawyers trying to decide whether to petition the court in the future on an problem that has been turned down one or more times.

    Question two: what roles do the law clerks and justices play?

    The answer is known to some extent but secret in other respects. For seven of the nine justices – all but Justices Samuel Alito and Neil Gorsuch – the initial review is by a single law clerk who writes a memo to be shared with the seven justices who participate in a “pool” for reviewing the petitions. Clerks to Alito and Gorsuch handle the petitions on their own.

    It has been revealed that but much about this aspect of the process remains hidden from public view. Little is known outside the court’s inner circle about how the clerks prepare their memos and what factors influence their recommendation to grant or deny review. The court’s own internal Rule 10 says the court is looking for cert. petitions that either present a conflict in which two or more lower courts have reached differing interpretations of an key issue of federal law, or which, even in the absence of a conflict, present an important question that the court should decide. But those factors alone do not guarantee cert. will be granted.

    In a recent development, just how influential the memo writer’s recommendation is on the judgment of the justices is also unknown. Nor is there any public knowledge of how often justices think the pool memo reached the wrong recommendation.

    Recent findings suggest that the cert. pool has been in use by the court for more than 50 years. The justices are certainly able to make adjustments if they find flaws in how it works, and the separate handling of petitions by Alito and Gorsuch provides some check on the process. But since this is largely an internal procedure of the court’s own making, it is not subject to any public accountability.

    According to recent reports, and the justices rarely discuss it. In his new book, for example, Alito makes no mention of the cert. process or the pool. Ultimately, little is known outside the court about how individual justices handle the pool memos.

    Question three: what influences the grant or denial or cert.?

    Many factors besides Rule 10 might contribute to whether a petition is granted. Law clerks may be influenced by whether any of the most respected, regular Supreme Court practitioners are involved in the case. Clients certainly think this matters, since they may spend thousands of dollars to hire firms with top Supreme Court practices, those that boast having former solicitors general and former law clerks to the justices as members of the firm.

    In a recent development, the clerks may also be swayed by what judges decided the case below, since some of them are especially respected in conservative or liberal circles. In certain instances, a federal appeals court may provide additional fodder to grant review. A party might have asked for rehearing by the full federal appeals court after losing in a three-judge panel. Such an “en banc” ruling, as it is called, can be especially influential, just as a set of opinions dissenting from denial of en banc review also tees up signals about the importance of a case.

    In a recent development, caution also plays a role here. No clerk wants to recommend that cert. be granted only to find that there are procedural flaws in a case (leading to it being “dismissed as improvidently granted”) or that the justices are not inclined to take up an especially ideologically divisive question.

    Question four: why are there so few cert. grants?

    In a recent development, the number of granted cases in recent years has reached the lowest level in many decades. At the height of the tenure of Chief Justice Warren Burger (1969-1986) in the 1980’s, the justices were deciding around 150 cases each term. Now the number is closer to 60.

    Oddly, no one seems to know why.

    There are some possible explanations, to be sure. One obvious factor is the rise of the interim docket, sometimes called the emergency or shadow docket. This docket involves interim requests for relief, where a party to a case asks the Supreme Court to block a lower court order in the interim period while the case is being litigated in a lower court. The Justice Department under President Donald Trump has used this path often, asking the justices to order that a Trump policy be allowed to remain in effect or to take effect after it was blocked by a federal judge.

    These interim orders, decided without full briefing and oral argument, are taking up an increasing amount of the court’s time, and some argue that this leaves less time for the justices to add more cert. petitions to be decided on their merits. While this is undoubtedly a factor, the number of cert. petitions being heard by the court each term has been shrinking for a long time, well before the significant uptick in interim docket matters.

    It has been revealed that different theories have been proffered by court observers for this decline over time: that Congress is passing fewer latest laws that lead to lawsuits and require judicial review; that there is less disagreement between conservative justices and conservative lower court judges, so less need for review; or even that the justices simply like having fewer cases to decide and therefore vote for cert. more sparingly.

    It is difficult to prove any one of these theories, and the justices are not providing any answers. In one case last spring involving a state court’s jurisdiction over a products liability lawsuit involving a organization based outside the state, counsel for both sides agreed that the court should hear and decide the concern (a rare occurrence, as the winner below typically argues against cert. being granted), but the justices still denied the petition. As is typically the case, there was no explanation.

    Question five: when does the court grant cert. before it is requested?

    The Supreme Court’s Rule 11 and federal law allow the justices to essentially reach out and grant review to a cert. petition before it has been decided by the appropriate appeals court; that is, before the appellate process has run its course. This once rarely used process has become a much more frequent tool for the justices. Whether they are following the guidance of the rule and focusing on “imperative public importance,” or whether they are impatient to tackle some major legal issues, or whether they simply think it will be more efficient to leapfrog over the court of appeals, the practice is clearly on the rise.

    Sources indicate that A recent example is Trump v. Slaughter, a fight over the independence of the heads of federal agencies from being fired by the president. The federal government came to the court for an interim stay of the ruling of a federal district court in the District of Columbia that blocked Trump from firing Rebecca Slaughter, a member of the Federal Trade Commission, because there was insufficient cause. The court granted the stay, allowing the firing to take effect, and then also granted cert. and ordered the case to be argued in December 2025.

    The process of granting review will continue unabated throughout the current court term. And as it does, questions will continue to arise about how the process works – but one should not hold their breath waiting for all the answers.

    Steve Wermiel is a professor of practice at American University Washington College of Law, where he has taught a seminar on the Supreme Court for nearly three decades.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Note, the release has been updated to include a quote from the National Security Division.

    An eight-count superseding indictment was unsealed today charging Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, with terrorism-related offenses for their activities in support of Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), two U.S. designated foreign terrorist organizations (FTOs), including their involvement in nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks throughout Europe and the United States, and a September 2026 terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, United Kingdom, where American armed forces were stationed.

    Sources indicate that “Anyone who intends a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “The defendants listed in the indictment allegedly supported two foreign terrorist organizations, and al-Saadi allegedly coordinated with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted terrorist plot. This Department of Justice will continue dismantling terrorist networks and protecting the American people from terrorist organizations.”.

    It has been revealed that “This eight-count indictment reveals the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the U.S., including one plot that was recently prevented at RAF Fairfield, a British Royal Air Force Base where American forces were stationed,” mentioned FBI Director Kash Patel. “According to the indictment, one of the subjects is behind bars awaiting trial yet he allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence. To date, the subjects have been allegedly involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks throughout Europe and the United States in support of Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (“IRGC”), two U.S. designated foreign terrorist organizations. This FBI will use all our resources to detect and stop such terrorist attacks as we’ve done the last 21 months – with over 1,300 terrorists disrupted and nearly 7,000 Foreign Terrorist Organization related arrests, up 1,057%. All those who threaten our homeland will get the message – justice will find you.”.

    “Today marks a major disruption of an alleged global terrorism conspiracy,” remarked Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “No matter where they are in the world, the National Security Division of the Department of Justice will pursue those who target American citizens and American interests. My thanks go out to the prosecutors and law enforcement partners for their work on this case.”.

    “As alleged, these defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” mentioned U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald for the Southern District of Fresh York. “Even after one of their co-conspirators was arrested and placed in federal custody, the defendants allegedly continued coordinating terrorist activity through coded communications and a network of associates overseas. The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real. Our Office will not stop working to address and disrupt this threat, and to prosecute those responsible.”.

    According to the allegations contained in the superseding indictment and other court filings: Al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri, and al-Hassani allegedly conspired to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the United States on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, both of which are FTOs. Most recently, in approximately September 2026, al-Hassani allegedly orchestrated a terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base (RAF Fairford) in Fairford, United Kingdom (the “RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot”), which at the time of the attempted attack, housed U.S. military aircraft and personnel.

    It has been revealed that al-Hassani and Mohajeri, both of whom were in Iran at the time of the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot, allegedly relied on a network of contacts in the United Kingdom. Al-Saadi, who was imprisoned and awaiting trial on pending terrorism charges in the Southern District of Newly introduced York, attempted to coordinate with al-Hassani and Mohajeri from jail by passing coded messages through third parties.

    It has been revealed that al-Saadi, a longtime operative of the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, was charged in May for working with and on behalf of the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, as well as other FTOs, for his involvement in planning and promoting approximately 18 terrorist attacks in Europe; and for attempting to bomb a synagogue in New York. The picture below shows al-Saadi in front of an array of machineguns in a conference room with a map of the United States on the wall next to a list of “legitimate targets” (redacted here) identifying former and current U.S. officials.

    As alleged, among the individuals with whom al-Saadi worked to facilitate and carry out the European Terrorist Attacks were Mohajeri and al-Hassani. Mohajeri is an Iranian national and operative of the IRGC who coordinated with al-Saadi and al-Hassani to carry out those terrorist attacks with the IRGC’s backing. Al-Hassani, who is originally from Iraq, used his contacts and criminal associates to carry out terrorist attacks in the United Kingdom.

    The European Terrorist Attacks were carried out in the name of a purportedly latest terrorist group with the pseudonym Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), which is a front for Kata’ib Hizballah and other FTOs. Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the United Kingdom, the most of any European country. The attacks involved arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual U.S.-British citizen.

    Al-Saadi, Mohajeri, and Al-Hassani were allegedly personally involved in planning many of the European Terrorist Attacks, and al-Saadi and Mohajeri helped create and publish online propaganda videos of these attacks. For example, on or about April 6, Mohajeri and al-Hassani planned attacks while together in a room in Iraq with a map of London displayed on a computer screen. In a video of that meeting, al-Hassani told Mohajeri, “we need to get focused on London.”  An image of the video is below, with Mohajeri on the right and al-Hassani on the left. HAYI then claimed responsibility for six terrorist attacks that occurred in and around London starting approximately one week later.

    Recent findings suggest that on or about April 17, al-Saadi, al-Hassani, and Mohajeri allegedly directed an individual to carry out one of the European Terrorist Attacks in real time. Specifically, al-Saadi, al-Hassani, and Mohajeri, along with others, were in a room watching a FaceTime video with the individual who was carrying out the attack, which was projected onto a large screen against the background of the HAYI logo. Al-Hassani directed the perpetrators’ actions, including by instructing the individual on the other end of the call to execute the attack and directing that individual to take a lighter and “light one in your hand,” “light it,” and “throw the fourth one.” Al-Saadi recorded the attack in real time, while Mohajeri recorded al-Hassani and al-Saadi in the room as they directed the attack. A still image from Mohajeri’s recording, showing al-Saadi (circled in red) and al-Hassani (circled in green), as they directed and filmed the attack, is below.

    The next day, on or about April 18, al-Hassani participated in another video call with an individual carrying out an attack on a synagogue in London, with the HAYI logo projected on the background of al-Hassani’s screen. During the video call, al-Hassani directed the individual to “light it up like a Christmas tree.” The person on the video then lit an improvised explosive device and threw it at a building. An image from the video is shown below.

    In March and April — overlapping with the time that al-Saadi was co-located in Iraq with Mohajeri and al-Hassani, planning the European Terrorist Attacks — al-Saadi allegedly attempted to coordinate and carry out terrorist attacks in the United States, including by targeting a synagogue in Manhattan.

    In a recent development, on or about May 1, following the European Terrorist Attacks, al-Saadi was arrested abroad and subsequently transferred to the custody of the United States to face prosecution. Al-Saadi has been in federal custody since his arrival in the United States. For approximately four months following al-Saadi’s arrest, there were no additional attacks attributable to al-Saadi, Mohajeri, and al-Hassani.

    In a recent development, in August, however, al-Hassani allegedly directed and paid associates in the United Kingdom to conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot. On Aug. 22, al-Hassani paid one individual (Individual-1) to perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford’s perimeter and al-Hassani subsequently received videos of the area surrounding the base. In later communications with al-Hassani, Individual-1 referred to him as “Ali.”.

    In September, al-Hassani also tasked and paid several individuals to help him prepare for the plot, including by procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel. At al-Hassani’s urging, those individuals commissioned custom decals that they affixed to the vans to create the appearance that they were used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business.

    On Sept. 26, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base. That day, al-Hassani was in frequent communication with the van drivers, helping to coordinate their movements and directing them where to drive. At least two of the three vans, while en route to the perimeter of RAF Fairford, encountered a security roadblock and were not allowed to proceed on their intended route. Al-Hassani communicated with the drivers and occupants of the vans both before and after encountering the security checkpoint. In the early morning hours of Sept. 27, law enforcement authorities in the United Kingdom recovered three white vans to which the fuel delivery business logos were affixed and arrested the occupants.

    Sources indicate that while in prison in Fresh York awaiting trial, al-Saadi has had phone calls with his immediate family members located in Iraq. As alleged, al-Saadi used those calls to pass coded messages to Mohajeri and al-Hassani in the days leading up to the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot.

    For example, in June and July, al-Saadi allegedly spoke with his mother and sister about Mohajeri. During those calls, they referred to Mohajeri by various aliases, including “Abbas, Abu Daniel” and “Sayyid Abbas.”  Al-Saadi also told his family members that he owed money to Mohajeri and directed them to pass along messages to Mohajeri about “work,” a term al-Saadi regularly used to describe terrorist activity, including on social media posts and in discussions with Mohajeri about partnering to conduct terrorist attacks. On one of those calls, al-Saadi also asked his sister, “What are they doing about all our old work?” and asked her whether it had been cancelled or just put on pause. Al-Saadi’s sister responded that “it isn’t cancelled.”.

    It has been revealed that on or about Sept. 24, al-Saadi once again spoke with his immediate family by phone. On the call, al-Saadi allegedly inquired about how al-Hassani, whom al-Saadi referred to as “Ali,” was doing. Al-Saadi’s family informed al-Saadi that “Ali” had been transferred to the “International Section.”  Al-Saadi then allegedly instructed his family to “give him [al-Hassani] money so we can do it.”  As described above, three days later, al-Hassani orchestrated the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot.

    Al-Saadi, 32, is a citizen of Iraq and Iran. Mohajeri, 48, is a citizen of Iran. Al-Hassani, 35, is a citizen of Iraq. A chart containing the names, charges, and minimum and maximum penalties for the defendants is set forth below.

    The Fourth District Court of Appeal in Florida on Wednesday banned a disbarred Florida attorney convicted of fraud from submitting pro se filings in his case after he allegedly “flooded” a trial court with documents, many generated with artificial intelligence.

    After Willie Joe Jones of Florida filed more than 70 documents with a circuit court since April 2025, a panel of judges ordered the clerk of the court to reject any of his future filings unless they are signed by a lawyer in good standing with the Florida Bar.

    “Abusive AI filing poses a serious threat to the orderly administration of justice,” the panel wrote.

    #90034. What is a discriminatory effect? The Montgomery County case and unpacking when schools may try for racial diversity without using race

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2438 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    What is a discriminatory effect? The Montgomery County case and unpacking when schools may try for racial diversity without using race

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2438 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.
    • Recent findings suggest that on Oct.
    • Industry observers note that in all of these cases, including this one, the policies at matter are facially neutral, meaning that a student’s race is not considered in the admissions process.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

    Recent findings suggest that on Oct. 19, the Supreme Court granted certiorari in Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education. The case is one of several in recent years dealing with magnet school admissions policies. While prior cases addressed the constitutional permissibility of changes to selection criteria at some of the nation’s most sought after public high schools like the Thomas Jefferson High School in northern Virginia and Stuyvesant High School and Bronx High School of Science in Upcoming York City, this case addresses whether changes to selection criteria for middle school magnet programs in Montgomery County, Maryland violates the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment.

    Industry observers note that in all of these cases, including this one, the policies at matter are facially neutral, meaning that a student’s race is not considered in the admissions process. As a result, the Supreme Court’s decision in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard is not directly relevant. In that case, the court held that using race as an explicit factor in the admissions process was unconstitutional.

    According to recent reports, at issue in this case is a change from one facially neutral admissions policy to another. During the pandemic, the school adopted the so-called “Pandemic Strategy.” Under the Pandemic Plan, all students are considered for admission to magnet schools if they meet minimum grade requirements and if their locally compared state assessment scores exceed a cut-off. Admission is then determined by a lottery from among those students who meet these requirements. Because schools in the region differ in their racial composition, basing admissions decisions on how well students score relative to other students in their same school ultimately affects the demographic composition of admitted students. AFEF claims that the Pandemic Plan violates equal protection because Montgomery County adopted it in order to change the racial demographics of the magnet schools and the plan had the effect of decreasing the share of Asian-American and white students.

    Industry observers note that according to the approach used by all of the courts evaluating magnet school admission practices, these facially neutral policies only violate equal protection if they are adopted for an impermissible reason (the intent element) and produce a discriminatory effect (the effect element). In AFEF v. Montgomery County, the district court found that the plaintiff had not alleged facts sufficient to satisfy either prong and so the school board’s motion to dismiss was granted. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit affirmed on the grounds that the district court properly evaluated whether there was a discriminatory effect.

    Sources indicate that when and why facially neutral policies violate equal protection is a hotly contested concern. Consider first the intent element. While all agree that the intention to exclude members of a particular racial group is invidious, there is disagreement about whether the intent to increase racial diversity is also impermissible. The Supreme Court has not yet directly ruled on this vital issue and will not do so in this case. The cert grant in AFEF v. Montgomery County focuses only on the second element: the discriminatory effect. In particular, the Supreme Court limited its grant of AFEF’s petition to the following question: “Whether a plaintiff challenging a facially neutral admissions policy as racially discriminatory must establish that the targeted racial group suffered an aggregate disparate impact relative to its share of the applicant pool.”.

    Industry observers note that this framing of the question roughly tracks the debate in the circuits between two different ways of showing discriminatory effect. In order to illustrate, let’s set aside the intent prong and assume it has been satisfied, either because the policy was actually adopted in order to reduce the percentage of Asian or white students in the magnet schools (though this fact is in dispute) or because the intention to increase the racial diversity of the schools is an impermissible intention (though this legal claim is contested). According to the 4th Circuit in Coalition for TJ v. Fairfax County and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit in Boston Parent Coalition for Academic Excellence Corp. v. School Committee for the City of Boston, the effect element would be satisfied if a lower percentage of Asian or white students are admitted than applied. For example, if Asian students represent 30% of the applicant pool but only 20% of the admitted class, this would constitute a discriminatory effect. However, if 40% of the admitted class are Asian, then no discriminatory effect would be found because Asian students would in this case constitute a higher percentage of the admitted class than their 30% share in the applicant pool. In AFEF v. Montgomery County, both the district court and the 4th Circuit followed this approach.

    By contrast, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit in Sargent v. School District of Philadelphia, the dissenting judge in Coalition for TJ, and Justice Samuel Alito in his dissent from the denial of cert. in that case, assess discriminatory effect differently. Rather than compare the percentage of admitted students of the race alleged to be intentionally excluded to their percentage in the wider applicant pool, these jurists look to see if there has been a decrease in the percentage of admitted students of this race under the newly introduced policy as compared to the prior policy. When a meaningful decrease is present, this constitutes a discriminatory effect. For example, if 50% of the admitted class were Asian under the prior policy and 40% are Asian under the new policy, this would constitute a discriminatory effect. And this would be so even if Asian students are still “overrepresented” in the sense that the percentage admitted is higher than their percentage of the applicant pool (30% in this example). In an article evaluating each of these approaches, we call this second approach the “Before-After Comparison” or “BAC,” and we call the first approach the “Population Comparison” or “PC.”.

    Yet both the PC and the BAC, as means of assessing discriminatory effect, have significant flaws. Let’s begin with the PC – the test used by the 4th and 1st Circuits. Recall that because the doctrine requires both impermissible intent and a discriminatory effect, it requires something more than just the fact that a policy is chosen for an invidious reason. The PC would effectively allow deliberate attempts to exclude Asians so long as they do well enough overall and do not fall below their share of the applicant pool. That seems problematic.

    Next consider the BAC, the test adopted by the 3rd Circuit, on which the discriminatory effect prong is satisfied only if the percentage of Asian students declines under the new policy. This test puts a strong thumb on the scale in favor of existing policies, whatever their merits, since sticking with the same policy is unlikely to result in major changes in the demographics of who is admitted. Thus a decision to keep things the same will evade scrutiny. And this is so even when maintaining a policy is done for uncontroversially bad reasons (say, because the existing policy is known to admit fewer Asian students, for example). In addition, the test is oversensitive to any changes in policy, since such changes are likely to lead to demographic shifts among the admitted students and thereby trigger a decrease for some group. While it is true that there will only be an equal protection violation if the school board at concern intended this decrease, it remains the case that any change at all is risky because the effect element will likely always be satisfied for some group. For both these reasons, the BAC privileges the status quo and makes change difficult by making the status quo policy the normative baseline.

    Sources indicate that the use of the term “aggregate” in the question on which certiorari was granted suggests that the court might think that the PC approach is flawed because it looks at how groups are treated rather than at how individuals are treated. And indeed it does. In AFEF v. Montgomery County, the discriminatory effect element would be satisfied (using the PC) if the percentage of Asian and white students admitted was lower than the percentage of these groups among the fifth-grade students in the county. But the BAC is no different in this respect. It too looks at how a racial group fares under the Pandemic Plan. The BAC would find discriminatory effect if the percentage of Asian students admitted under the Pandemic Plan is less than the percentage admitted under the approach that preceded it. In other words, both tests for discriminatory effect focus on how the racial groups who are alleged to be the target of the invidious intentions fare as groups.

    Sources indicate that can either of these tests be reframed in ways that focus on how an individual is treated, rather than how members of her racial group are treated? After all, equal protection doctrine has long emphasized that the clause protects individuals rather than groups. Unfortunately, this is not easy to do. If a school uses race to decide which students to admit, it makes sense to say that a student’s race played a role in how she was treated. Facially neutral policies are different, however. Consider a simple and familiar facially neutral policy. Suppose a school board decides to admit the top 2% of each middle school to its coveted magnet high school. Suppose also that it does so, at least in part, to increase the racial diversity of the magnet school. Because there are more black and Latino students in some middle schools and more Asian and white students in others, this policy then produces a magnet school class that has a significant number of students of all races, let us suppose. Now consider an Asian student who is denied admissions because she is not in the top 2% of her middle school class. Has she been denied admission “because of her race?”.

    Industry observers note that one answer to this question could be simply “no.” Any student rejected by the admissions policy suffers a harm. It is this harm that gives the student standing to sue. But this rejection is not based on the student’s race when the school’s admissions policy is facially neutral. If this is correct (and if aggregate tests are out), then the court’s only option is to jettison the effect prong of the claim altogether. Were the court to take this route, facially neutral laws or policies would violate equal protection solely on the grounds that they were adopted with invidious intent.

    Recent findings suggest that the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 2nd Circuit attempts a different approach. It uses the BAC to explain how individual students have suffered a discriminatory effect under a facially neutral policy. In Chinese American Citizens Alliance of Greater Fresh York v. Adams, the percentage of Asian students admitted under the challenged admissions policy remained higher than their percentage in the applicant pool (thus failing to satisfy the PC in its aggregate form) and also did not decrease as compared to the prior admissions policy (thus failing to satisfy the BAC in its aggregate form). Yet the 2nd Circuit held that the effect element “can be satisfied by proof of an adverse harm to one or more individuals based on their race that has resulted from that discriminatory law or policy” (emphasis added). But the crucial question remains: in what way were the rejected Asian students rejected “because of their race” when race did not affect these decisions since the policy is facially neutral? The 2nd Circuit answers that question by referring to the fact that these students were “qualified for admission on an individual basis under the previous criteria" (emphasis added). In other words, in the view of the 2nd Circuit, if a new policy is adopted to exclude Asian students, then those Asian students who would have been admitted under the previous policy are denied admission because of their race.

    It has been revealed that this approach can be understood as an attempt to make the BAC individualized: the court here is determining whether a student’s rejection constitutes a distinctively discriminatory harm by drawing a comparison with how she would have fared under the previous policy. If this approach works (which we are agnostic about) for the BAC, a similar approach can be tailored for the PC as well. Here is how that would go. If a facially neutral policy was adopted in order to exclude Asian students and that policy is one under which Asian students are admitted at lower rates than students of other races, then each Asian student subject to that policy is subject to a policy that makes it harder for them to be admitted than it is for students of other races. On this view, each Asian student denied admission using this policy is then denied admission based on their race.

    In a recent development, thus, both tests can be articulated such that they capture a way that individual students are rejected based on their race. For this reason, the court should not choose one approach over the other on the grounds that one frames the injury in individual terms and the other looks at how groups are treated.

    This leaves the court with two options. First, as mentioned earlier, it could jettison the effect prong of the claim entirely and conclude that bad intentions alone render a facially neutral admissions policy impermissible. Doing so would put more pressure on the importance of answering the question of what intentions are invidious and, in particular, whether the intent to increase racial diversity is itself unconstitutional. Alternatively, the court must confront the question of discriminatory harm head-on and assess whether the BAC or PC provides the better account of it.

    Sources indicate that deborah Hellman is the Robert E. Scott Distinguished Professor of Law and the Honorable Albert V. Bryan Jr. ’50 Professor of Law at the University of Virginia School of Law, as well as Director of their Center for Law & Philosophy.

    Lily Hu is an Assistant Professor of Philosophy at Yale University and also a contributing editor at Boston Review.

    #90029. Latest Update: Justice Department Reveals Actions to Disrupt North Korea’s Massive Theft of Cryptocurrency

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1304 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fbi ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Justice Department Reveals Actions to Disrupt North Korea’s Massive Theft of Cryptocurrency

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1304 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fbi

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency.
    • It has been revealed that “North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” stated Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M.
    • “The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” remarked Assistant Attorney General A.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency. These actions include the seizure of cloud-based infrastructure used in the FaceStealer social engineering scheme that has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency and the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance, a virtual currency exchange.

    It has been revealed that “North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” stated Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “Today’s announcement reveals that America will fight back against that corrupt regime’s effort to profit through cybercrime. The National Security Division will use every tool at its disposal to seize and return North Korea’s ill-gotten gains.”.

    “The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” remarked Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “As the Department’s liaison to the digital asset industry, the Criminal Division swiftly and efficiently used its expertise to immediately halt about half of this historic breach.”.

    In a recent development, “Cryptocurrency unfortunately has become fertile ground for North Korea to defraud victims and fund its malign activities,” stated First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California. “Today’s seizure shows that America will continue the fight against rogue states who financially gain from cybercrime.”.

    It has been revealed that “By springing into action at a moment’s notice, we worked together to freeze this massive criminal fraud in its tracks,” stated U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “The North Korean regime may think they are sophisticated cyber criminals, but we have consistently met them head on, as we did here seizing more than $1.2 billion of their stolen assets.”.

    Industry observers note that “The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years,” noted FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman. “North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months. The FBI remains committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing cost on North Korean actors targeting the virtual asset community.”.

    “North Korea’s FaceStealer is a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user” stated Assistant Director in Charge Patrick Grandy of the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office. “It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships. If you can’t imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough. The FBI is sounding the alarm to elevate awareness of this growing scheme, now aimed not only at crypto theft, but also the exploitation of the of the open-source software supply chain.”.

    Seizure of FaceStealer Infrastructure – Central District of California.

    It has been revealed that today, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California announced the disruption of cloud-based infrastructure used by North Korean hackers in a highly effective social engineering scheme that the FBI is calling “FaceStealer.” The scheme, which relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and artificial deepfakes, has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months and the attempted compromise of individuals involved in the open-source software supply chain.

    North Korean hackers known publicly by the names Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Dangerous Password, CryptoCore, Advanced Persistent Threat 38 (APT38), BlueNoroff, and Stardust Chollima have lured targets with invitations to video meetings delivered from accounts stolen from prior victims. Once a target joins the meeting, the hackers record the target’s webcam video and play a prerecorded video of a previous victim or victims known to the target, thereby simulating the participation of trusted contacts in the meeting to gain the target’s trust. The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective. Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target’s trust.

    Industry observers note that during the meeting, the hackers then introduce a fake technical error into the meeting, such as claiming that the target cannot be heard, and provide a link or prompt to fix the error. The “fix” surreptitiously installs malware on the target’s computer. With the target’s computer compromised, the hackers can steal cryptocurrency or exploit the target’s access to other computer infrastructure. In several reported cases, the hackers stole cryptocurrency and hijacked communication accounts several months to more than a year after the initial compromise. As part of the scheme the hackers also accessed the new victim’s contact lists, social media, and communications apps to target the victim’s personal and professional contacts.

    Recent findings suggest that the North Korean hackers target individuals working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries. Additionally, they have increasingly targeted individuals involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software with the FaceStealer technique, attempting to gain access to their devices and the software repository accounts they control. This targeting appears calculated to enable software supply-chain attacks. Pursuant to a federal warrant, the FBI seized over 900 webcam videos of FaceStealer victims.

    It has been revealed that the FBI today published a report providing greater detail on the mechanics of the FaceStealer scheme, including best practices to protect against this scheme and steps victims can take in the event of a compromise. Additionally, the FBI created a website, www.fbi.gov/facestealer, to serve as a centralized hub for resources and information on the scheme.

    The effort to disrupt the FaceStealer campaign was led by Assistant U.S. Attorney Khaldoun Shobaki for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

    The Department, FBI, and Law Enforcement Partners Interdict More Than a Billion Dollars Worth of Virtual Assets Stolen From Binance.

    Separately from the FaceStealer campaign, on or about Oct. 29, members of the North Korean military, referred to by the FBI as “TraderTraitor” stole more than $6 billion worth of virtual assets from the Binance cryptocurrency exchange. Since the theft, the National Security Division’s National Security Cyber Section, the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, and law enforcement partners have worked closely with virtual asset service providers (VASPs) to interdict the stolen assets. Collective U.S. government and private sector efforts so far have resulted in the freeze of more than $2.7 billion, with the Department having already obtained court-authorization to seize or restrain in excess of $1.2 billion of that amount.

    Recent findings suggest that efforts to trace, freeze, seize, and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder such assets through various cryptocurrency bridges, mixers, and exchanges. For example, last week, the FBI, in coordination with its law enforcement partners at the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS-CI), issued a Cyber Alert attributing the theft and urging VASPs to block transactions with or derived from cryptocurrency addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder the stolen Binance assets.

    The FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, Cyber Division, and Virtual Asset Unit are coordinating the FBI’s efforts to recover the stolen virtual assets, working in partnership with the USSS and the IRS-CI.

    #90028. The major Trump cases that might come back to SCOTUS

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2719 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    The major Trump cases that might come back to SCOTUS

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Supreme Court heard three oral arguments this week, wrapping up the November argument session.
    • Recent findings suggest that today, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review.
    • On Thursday, the Supreme Court denied a request for a stay of execution from James Pavatt, who was sentenced to death for the 2001 murder of Rob Andrew.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Supreme Court heard three oral arguments this week, wrapping up the November argument session. It also decided an interim docket case on border wall construction in southwestern Texas, granting the Trump administration’s request to be allowed to continue construction in an apparent 8-1 vote.

    Recent findings suggest that today, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. Orders from today’s conference are expected on Monday at 9:30 a.m. EST.

    On Thursday, the Supreme Court denied a request for a stay of execution from James Pavatt, who was sentenced to death for the 2001 murder of Rob Andrew. Just over an hour later, Pavatt was executed in Oklahoma.

    Recent findings suggest that on Tuesday, the justices heard oral argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, LLC, on whether the Constitution allows the executive branch – as opposed to the courts – to adjudicate an employer’s obligation to comply with employment agreements concerning temporary immigrant workers. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

    On Monday, the justices heard argument in Nielsen v. Watanabe, on whether and when federal officials can be held liable for constitutional violations. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

    Also on Monday, the justices heard argument in Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc., on whether the “just compensation” paid to land owners losing property to a pipeline project should be determined by referring to state law, which often provides for a higher payment than what the Constitution requires. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

    It has been revealed that later on Monday, the Supreme Court granted the Trump administration’s request to be allowed to resume construction of its border wall in the Massive Bend region of southwestern Texas. Only Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated, without explanation, that she would have denied the government’s request.

    According to recent reports, in Monday’s order list, the Supreme Court denied review in over 200 cases, including disputes involving the George Floyd protests in Minneapolis, actor Randy Quaid, and the sons of former baseball player Roberto Clemente. It also asked the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a case over whether U.S. terrorism victims may sue 21 pharmaceutical and medical-device companies under the Antiterrorism Act for allegedly aiding and abetting Iraqi terrorists.

    Industry observers note that in early October, a high school wrestler in Washington state and her mother came to the Supreme Court’s interim docket and asked the justices to prevent transgender girls from competing against her during this year’s wrestling season. The application has been fully briefed since Oct. 15, but the Supreme Court has not yet taken action. In a Monday letter, the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association asked the court not to intervene, highlighting the passage last week of a ballot initiative in Washington that aims to prevent “biologically male students from competing with and against female students in athletic activities that have separate classifications for male and female students” at K-12 schools.

    While speaking to the Federalist Society on Thursday, Justice Samuel Alito “warned against any potential congressional action to defund the Supreme Court as he defended the importance of an independent judiciary,” according to The Hill. “Congress can turn off the lights at the Supreme Court and stop everything from happening if they want to defund their activities,” he remarked. “So, it is notable to preserve the independence of the judiciary. If that is eliminated, then the Constitution as adopted in 1789 will no longer be the same.” He also described the judicial branch as “the least powerful branch,” adding that “it is ‘vulnerable’ to Congress and the executive.” But that doesn’t mean judges can’t go too far, Alito added. “If you think about a hand grenade, a 500-pound bomb and a nuclear weapon,” he said, “the hand grenade is the least dangerous. But that is not to say that it is not dangerous.”.

    In February, “the Supreme Court struck down tariffs President Donald Trump imposed last year under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act,” holding that the law does not grant the president the power to impose tariffs. The next month, the U.S. Court of International Trade “ordered Customs and Border Patrol to problem refunds to importers totaling about $166 billion.” Now, seven Senate Democrats are asking the Federal Trade Commission “to investigate whether large corporations that received billions of dollars in tariff refunds violated federal law by not passing them on to their customers,” according to USA Today. “By increasing consumer prices, ostensibly due to tariff costs, and then refusing to provide refunds to consumers when they are later reimbursed for those tariff costs,” the senators wrote, “corporations may be in violation of the” Federal Trade Commission Act, which “empowers the commission to prevent ‘unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.’”.

    In a recent development, during a Thursday panel at the Federalist Society’s annual National Lawyers Convention, “White House counsel Will Scharf praised the Supreme Court’s June decision strengthening presidential firing power as a ‘generational win’” that “righted what he viewed as a ‘historic constitutional wrong,’” according to The Hill. “A president who can’t control who’s exercising the executive power that is vested in him, that’s a cabined presidency,” Scharf noted. “The Supreme Court did a masterful job,” he added. “Really got it right.”.

    Sources indicate that on Thursday, former death row inmate Richard Glossip appeared in Oklahoma County District Court “for what was supposed to be his second hearing on pretrial motions” in the state’s effort to retry him for the 1997 murder of Barry Van Treese. “However, the hearing took a turn when the state unveiled an agreement between the prosecution and the defense,” under which “Glossip pleaded guilty to one count of accessory to murder,” according to KOKH in Oklahoma City. The plea agreement comes after the Supreme Court in 2025 “threw out Glossip’s murder conviction and death sentence,” determining that prosecutors had failed to correct false testimony. “Glossip’s sentencing is set for Dec. 17 and Dec. 18.”.

    Adam Liptak, The Upcoming York Times.

    In his newsletter for The Upcoming York Times, Adam Liptak highlighted “hurdles and roadblocks [] erected by the Supreme Court” that may stand in the way of at least some of the new Congress’ planned investigations into “the Trump administration and its allies.” For example, in 2024’s Trump v. United States, in which the court granted the president “substantial immunity from prosecution, Chief Justice John Roberts indicated that some subjects may be entirely off limits to congressional investigators.” “Those subjects included issuing pardons, firing subordinates and deciding ‘which crimes to investigate and prosecute.’” It is also significant, according to Liptak, that “the court has never definitively resolved” whether Congress can “sue the executive branch,” an matter that will likely arise if the administration refuses “to give Congress documents or let officials testify.” Liptak noted that “it is not at all clear that the Supreme Court would be willing to mediate” disputes between Congress and the executive branch over access to information, “or if the justices would side with the Democratic Congress if it does.”.

    During the 2025-26 term, the Supreme Court handed President Donald Trump defeats in cases on birthright citizenship, tariffs, and his effort to fire Lisa Cook. But those rulings do not necessarily mean the justices have seen the last of any of those concerns.

    In his Nuts and Bolts column, Stephen Wermiel explored how the Supreme Court decides what cases to decide, also known as the certiorari or “cert.” process. According to him, “questions will continue to arise about how th[is] process works – but one should not hold their breath waiting for all the answers.”.

    In a column for SCOTUSblog, Deborah Hellman and Lily Hu revisited the Supreme Court’s decision to grant review in Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education, a case on the circumstances under which facially neutral admissions policies violate equal protection by producing a discriminatory effect.

    In his Relist Watch column on Wednesday, John Elwood explored 11 petitions for review that will get a second look from the justices during today’s conference, which cover such issues as the Trump administration’s effort to remove certain noncitizens from the country without first allowing them to apply for asylum and a ban on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.”.

    In his Born Free and Equal column on Wednesday, Steven Calabresi reviewed Justice Samuel Alito’s new book and commended it as “exceptionally intellectual and provocative.” “The book fills the shoes of the late Justice Scalia, and I would recommend it to everyone – whether they agree with Justice Alito’s jurisprudence or not,” Calabresi concluded.

    On Tuesday, Amy reported that the Trump administration has once again asked the Supreme Court to intervene in its efforts to build a fresh White House ballroom. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the justices that the project “should be permitted to move forward outside the shadow of judicial superintendence.”.

    It has been revealed that in her inaugural Substance and Procedure column on Monday, Rachel Bayefsky explored the Supreme Court’s application of a “history-and-tradition” analysis in recent cases on the constitutionality of agency adjudication – that is, “the practice of resolving disputes ‘in-house’ within administrative agencies instead of addressing” them in a court. According to Bayefsky, the court’s decision in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards “may have an vital impact not only on the future of agency adjudication, but also on the trajectory of historically driven interpretation across a variety of pressing constitutional debates.”.

    Recent findings suggest that sarah Isgur and David French analyze free speech complications from the past three election cycles, including Donald Trump’s “they/them” ad in 2024 and the Trump administration’s threats to social media companies. They then discuss a free speech fight that may define the next two years.

    The Closer Look in Friday editions is typically a judicial biography. This week, we cover Justice Samuel Nelson, who served on the court from 1845 to 1872.

    It has been revealed that while you might think there’s only one justice with the name Samuel based on recent news coverage, there have actually been five with that first name in the court’s history – and in today’s justice biography, we’ll take a look at the second. (The first, if you recall, didn’t get things off to a particularly great start: He is the only justice to have been impeached.).

    In a recent development, although referred to as “one of those nineteenth-century justices of whom we often lose sight” (the Journal of Supreme Court History remarked it, not us), Justice Samuel Nelson served on the court for 27 years as a “pragmatic yet low-key man,” as described by Oyez. Things began for him in Hebron, Upcoming York, where he was born in November 1792 to Scot-Irish farmers. His father helped pay Nelson’s Middlebury College tuition by selling a person who was enslaved. Nelson graduated from Middlebury in 1813; clerked at a Salem law firm; followed one of its partners to Madison County, New York when the firm split; and was admitted to the bar in 1817 (two years later, he married his law firm practice partner’s daughter).

    In 1820, Nelson was appointed the town’s postmaster and served as a presidential elector for James Monroe. He became a delegate to the 1821 state constitutional convention, where he pushed to eliminate property requirements for male voters.

    According to recent reports, latest York Gov. Joseph Yates appointed Nelson as a state circuit judge in 1823. Gov. Enos Throop elevated him to the New York Supreme Court of Judicature (that state’s highest trial court) in 1831, and he became its chief justice in 1837. In Jack v. Martin, he held that New York could not interfere with enforcement of the federal Fugitive Slave Act and noted that anyone who seized a free man would, under state law, “be answerable like any other trespasser or kidnapper.”.

    Sources indicate that in 1845, Nelson ran for the U.S. Senate and lost. Shortly after, President John Tyler nominated him to succeed Justice Smith Thompson. The Senate confirmed Nelson by voice vote in February 1845, and he served as circuit justice for the 2nd Circuit (Connecticut, Upcoming York, and Vermont) while on the Supreme Court.

    On the bench, Nelson “kept a low profile,” generally voting with the majority. He did write a few notable decisions, one of them in 1850’s Hotchkiss v. Greenwood, a landmark patent law case. In 1857’s Fellows v. Blacksmith, Nelson wrote for a unanimous court that a land organization could not forcibly evict the Tonawanda Senecas, calling such litigation “appalling.” According to one scholar, Nelson “persuaded all his brethren, including those who had supported Jacksonian Indian removal policies, of the merits of the Tonawandas’ Seneca treaty arguments.” The same scholar wrote that Fellows eventually allowed for the treaty that let the tribe buy back 7,500 acres of its reservation.

    In a recent development, fellows was decided the same year as Dred Scott v. Sandford. Nelson reportedly resisted behind-the-scenes pressure from incoming President James Buchanan to endorse at least part of Chief Justice Roger Taney’s opinion (unlike Justice Robert Grier). Nevertheless, he concurred with the majority, and scholars have “castigat[ed] him, along with Justice Robert Grier of Pennsylvania, for being the only two Northern jurists on the bench who voted with the majority in the case.” (Ten years later in Georgia v. Stanton, Nelson refused to let Georgia block Congress’ Reconstruction program, holding that its claims “call for the judgment of the court upon political questions.”).

    In the lead-up to the Civil War, Nelson and Justice John Campbell acted as intermediaries between Secretary of State William Seward and Southern commissioners who wanted the Confederacy recognized. Privately, Nelson wrote on Christmas Day in 1860 that “we almost despair of the republic” and in 1862 wrote to Justice Benjamin Curtis that he hoped the country might survive both “the fierceness of the enemy without and imbecility of the authorities within.”.

    According to recent reports, nelson also dissented in the 1863 Prize Cases, arguing that President Abraham Lincoln could not legally blockade Southern ports until Congress declared war. The dissent (along with his vote in Ex parte Milligan to overturn the conviction of a man charged with helping the Confederacy and opposing expanding federal power) led critics to question his loyalty to the Union.

    Following the civil war, President Ulysses S. Grant in 1871 named the 79-year-old Nelson one of five American members of the commission handling claims against Great Britain for the damages caused by British-built Confederate ships, which Nelson accepted (although he wrote that he was “hardly at liberty to refuse”). The proceedings won the United States $15.5 million.

    Sources indicate that nelson retired in November 1872. He died in Cooperstown, New York, in December 1873, at age 81. One historian wrote that Nelson was a “quietly competent jurist” in comparison to several of “his more flamboyant and controversial judicial brethren” (some of whom we will be covering soon).

    On Nov. 10, Judge Richard Posner passed away at the age of 87. Posner, who served on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit from 1981 to 2017, was one of the most influential jurists never to have served on the Supreme Court. In addition to his voluminous opinions (some affirmed, others denied), Posner authored over 60 books and more than 500 articles and served as a Senior Lecturer in Law at the University of Chicago Law School. Among his many contributions, Posner helped give life to the law and economics movement and to the study of judging as an empirical pursuit. As Zach, our executive editor, can attest to first-hand, he was both charming and hilarious in person and did not suffer bad ideas lightly. But this is SCOTUSblog. So what did Posner have to say about the court specifically? Here are some choice quotations (you may notice a theme):.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, also known as “Chapo Isidro,” an alleged leader of the Sinaloa Cartel, has been captured by the Mexican military following a Homeland Security Task Force Investigation.

    Industry observers note that “We commend Mexico’s military and special forces on last night’s capture of Sinaloa Cartel senior leader ‘Chapo Isidro,’ remarked Attorney General Todd Blanche. “A combined interagency effort, including the Homeland Security Task Force, supported this Mexican operation to remove a leader of one of the most dangerous drug cartels in Mexico. This successful operation is the result of a bilateral effort to eliminate terrorists in Mexico. We extend our condolences to the families of the elite soldiers who were killed and our gratitude to the Mexican government.”.

    Sources indicate that “The arrest of Chapo Isidro demonstrates the outstanding strength and reach of the Homeland Security Task Force,” said Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin. “Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and our HSTF partners relentlessly pursued one of the world’s most dangerous cartel leaders, whose organization is alleged to have flooded our communities with deadly narcotics and terrorized communities through extreme violence. This operation sends an unmistakable message, cartel leaders cannot hide behind borders, money, or brutality. The Homeland Security Task Force will continue its work to dismantle these criminal and terrorist networks, hold their leaders accountable, and protect the American people.”.

    Meza Flores was captured on November 20 in a spectacular military operation in Guasave, Sinaloa, Mexico, that also resulted in the arrest of alleged cartel leader German Rolando Galvez Meza, also known as “El Serafin.”.

    A federal grand jury in the District of Columbia returned a second superseding indictment on September 25 charging Meza-Flores, 44, of Sonora, Mexico, with conspiracy to provide material support to a terrorist organization, narcoterrorism, conducting a continuing criminal enterprise, money laundering and firearms related charges. The case is being prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of California and the Justice Department’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section.

    Recent findings suggest that the Sinaloa Cartel is one of the most prolific and dangerous drug cartels in Mexico, known for its widespread use of corruption and violence to further its drug trafficking activities. On February 20, 2025, the U.S. Secretary of State designated the Cartel de Sinaloa as a Foreign Terrorist Organization (FTO) under Section 219 of the Immigration and Nationality Act and as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist under Executive Order 13224. The Secretary of State has also listed the following aliases for the Cartel de Sinaloa: Sinaloa Cartel, Mexican Federation, and Guadalajara Cartel.

    In a recent development, according to court documents, under Meza Flores’s leadership, the Sinaloa Cartel produced and trafficked multi-tonnage quantities of drugs, including cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin, marijuana, and fentanyl into the United States, and used extreme violence to further its operations. Meza Flores commanded a large contingent of gunmen to control significant territory in the Guasave, Los Mochis, and remote Sinaloa mountains. The cartel uses this territory to manufacture and distribute illicit controlled substances, transporting them north to the United States. It is further alleged that Meza Flores has engaged in continual and extreme violence, including (1) murdering rival cartel members in public; (2) kidnapping, torturing, and murdering rival cartel members at camps and elsewhere; (3) kidnapping, torturing, and murdering members of the Mexican police; and (4) terrorizing the people of Mexico.

    Recent findings suggest that “Meza Flores is on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives List for a reason; he is the most dangerous man in Mexico,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “For decades Meza Flores has promoted the terrorist objectives of the Sinaloa Cartel, promoting unparalleled violence throughout southern Mexico and flooding the United States with deadly substances all in the name of profit. With this indictment made possible by the Homeland Security Task Force, subsequent arrest and the continued support of our Mexican partners, we aim to bring him to justice and fully dismantle this cartel.”.

    According to recent reports, “Chapo Isidro built an empire in the shadows. Today’s sunrise was his sunset,” said U.S. Attorney Adam Gordon for the Southern District of California.

    According to recent reports, “Another FBI Ten Most Wanted fugitive is off the board,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” has been captured by Mexican forces with U.S. assistance. This alleged cartel leader is accused of flooding American communities with deadly drugs, including fentanyl. This is the 11th Ten Most Wanted fugitive captured under the Trump Administration. Outstanding work by our law enforcement partners in Mexico and everyone involved in this operation. Under President Trump’s leadership, this FBI will continue relentlessly pursuing the criminals and cartels poisoning our communities and threatening American lives.”.

    “Homeland Security Investigations is proud of the exceptional work of our special agents and personnel across our domestic and international offices whose determination, expertise, and coordination through the HSTF helped bring Chapo Isidro to justice,” stated HSI Acting Executive Associate Director John A. Condon. “Working alongside our HSTF partners, HSI investigated this dangerous cartel leader and helped dismantle the criminal enterprise he allegedly used to poison American communities and fuel brutal violence. This arrest demonstrates the reach of HSI’s global investigative authorities and the strength of the HSTF as partners work together to take coordinated and relentless action against transnational criminal organizations that threaten our homeland.”.

    Meza Flores is charged in a six-count superseding indictment filed in the District of Columbia with leading a continuing criminal enterprise, conspiracy to manufacture and distribute cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin, marijuana, and fentanyl for importation into the United States, international money laundering conspiracy, conspiracy to provide material support to a terrorist organization, narcoterrorism, and using a firearm including a machinegun and a destructive device.

    If convicted of these charges, Meza Flores faces the death penalty or a mandatory term of life in prison.

    According to recent reports, the U.S. Department of State is offering a reward of up to $5 million for information that led to the arrest and/or will lead to the conviction of Chapo Isidro. If you have any information concerning Chapo Isidro, please contact your local FBI office or the nearest American Embassy or Consulate or call the FBI at 1-800-CALL-FBI (1-800-225-5324). You can also submit a tip online at tips.fbi.gov  See: https://www.state.gov/fausto-isidro-meza-flores.

    Recent findings suggest that the HSTF including FBI Washington and San Diego Field Offices and HSI San Diego investigated the case with significant assistance from DEA, ATF, and the U.S. Marshals Service.

    Deputy Chief James Hepburn and Trial Attorney Jayce Born of the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section (MNF) and Assistant U.S. Attorney Joshua Mellor of the Southern District of California are prosecuting the case. The Justice Department's National Security Division, Office of International Affairs and Capital Case Section provided significant assistance.

    In a recent development, the Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section’s (MNF) mission is to take the profit out of crime, eliminate drug cartels, and protect the U.S. financial system. MNF pursues criminal prosecutions and criminal and civil asset recovery actions involving: financial facilitators who launder profits for criminals; financial institutions and their officers and employees whose actions threaten the U.S. financial system and financial institutions; international money launderers who support transnational organized crime; and the top command and control of international drug trafficking organizations.

    MNF’s Narcotic and Dangerous Drug Unit investigates and prosecutes the top command and control elements of international drug cartels, drug trafficking organizations, and related transnational criminal organizations.

    Sources indicate that this case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of U.S. law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States.

    • Upcoming research from Stanford University has found that people are increasingly using artificial intelligence to file lawsuits.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, newly introduced research from Stanford University has found that people are increasingly using artificial intelligence to file lawsuits. (Photo by Userba011d64_201/Getty Images).

    Upcoming research from Stanford University has found that people are increasingly using artificial intelligence to file lawsuits.

    According to recent reports, according to the report, which was released by the university’s researchers Thursday, more than a third of civil suits filed in Santa Clara County, California, and San Francisco County this year show signs of AI use. The researchers noted that this doesn’t include debt collection cases.

    Among other findings, Stanford’s researchers noted that pro se litigants had higher AI adoption rates. In Santa Clara County, the share of self-represented complaints that showed signs of AI use increased from 19% in 2024 to 72% in 2026. Meanwhile, the share of attorney-filed complaints increased from 5% to 34% during this period.

    According to recent reports, researchers also found that the use of AI varies by case type, with employment and business complaints in California showing the highest rates. They remarked AI use also varies throughout court filings, with more appearances in the statement of facts and causes of actions sections.

    “The sharp rise we document here corroborates that AI in the law is a question of how, not whether,” Stanford’s researchers wrote in the report.

    #90011. Tribal property and the Supreme Court

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1132 w)
